113768.q: How did Hermann Ebbinghaus test how quickly we forget what we have learnt?
a: He learnt meaningless syllables by heart himself
He watched rats in the laboratory
He took pictures of the brain
113768.e: In experiments on himself, Hermann Ebbinghaus learnt meaningless syllables and checked how much he still knew later. This led to the forgetting curve.
113768.m: Ebbinghaus studied how quickly we forget.

113769.q: What does the forgetting curve show?
a: You forget the most shortly after learning
You forget the same amount every day
You only forget after a year
What you learn is never forgotten
113769.e: Right after learning, how much you remember drops steeply, and later only slowly. That is why it pays to revise early.
113769.m: Without revision, you forget most things soon after learning them.

113770.q: According to research, which learning strategy is usually more effective?
a: Revising the material spread over several days
Learning everything in one long night before the test
Reading it once and never revising
Only learning on the day of the test
113770.e: Spread-out learning with breaks leads to better remembering than cramming everything at once. Experts call this the spacing effect.
113770.m: If you spread out your revision, you remember more.

113771.q: What did the famous Bobo doll experiment show?
a: Children copy what adults show them
Children forget what they see at once
113771.e: Children watched a film in which an adult hit a doll. Afterwards, many of the children copied this behaviour. The psychologist Albert Bandura called this learning from a model.
113771.m: Children learn a lot by copying role models.

113772.q: A dog gets a treat every time it sits down. Soon it sits down much more often. How has it learnt this?
113772.e: A behaviour becomes more frequent when it is rewarded and less frequent when it is punished. Experts call this operant conditioning.
113772.m: Rewarded behaviour is shown more often.

113773.q: What did animals learn in the so-called Skinner box?
a: To press a lever to get food
To recognise themselves in a mirror
113773.e: In the Skinner box, rats or pigeons learnt to press a lever or peck a key to get food. This allowed Burrhus F. Skinner to measure learning precisely.
113773.m: In the Skinner box, animals learnt through food rewards.

113774.q: What does learning by trial and error mean?
a: You keep trying things until something works
You read the whole instructions first
113774.e: When learning by trial and error, you try out different ways. You keep what works, and with every attempt you get faster.
113774.m: Through trial and error, you get faster over time.

113775.q: According to research on learning, what helps more than just reading something through several times?
a: Copying out the text in colour
Listening to loud music at the same time
113775.e: When you test yourself, you have to actively bring the knowledge back from memory. This strengthens the memory more than reading passively.
113775.m: Testing yourself makes learning last longer.

113776.q: Whom did the greylag goslings follow that Konrad Lorenz saw first after hatching?
113776.e: Young geese follow the first moving creature they see shortly after hatching. Lorenz called this kind of learning imprinting.
113776.m: In imprinting, young animals learn within a short time whom to follow.

113777.q: What do you call a stimulus that causes a reaction without any learning?
113777.e: A puff of air into the eye, for example, makes you blink without any learning. Stimuli like this are called unconditioned stimuli.
113777.m: An unconditioned stimulus works without any previous learning.

113778.q: What is it called when a learnt reaction disappears because the stimulus keeps occurring for a long time without the reward?
113778.e: If nothing follows the learnt stimulus again and again, the reaction becomes weaker. Experts call this extinction.
113778.m: Without the link, a learnt reaction becomes weaker.

113779.q: A dog has unlearnt drooling at the sound of a bell. What can still happen after a longer break?
a: It suddenly drools briefly at the sound again
It becomes afraid of the bell
It no longer hears the bell
113779.e: A reaction that has been unlearnt is not completely forgotten. After a break, it can briefly come back. Experts call this spontaneous recovery.
113779.m: Unlearnt reactions can come back after a break.

113780.q: In an experiment in 1920, which animal did “Little Albert” learn to be afraid of?
113780.e: Every time the toddler saw the rat, a loud bang was made. Soon he was afraid of the rat on its own. Today the experiment is seen as unethical.
113780.m: Fear can also be learnt through conditioning.

113781.q: A child has learnt to be afraid of one particular dog. What often happens?
a: It is also afraid of similar dogs
It is only afraid of that one dog
It suddenly likes all dogs especially
It is now only afraid of cats
113781.e: A learnt fear often spreads to similar stimuli. This is called stimulus generalisation.
113781.m: Similar stimuli can set off the same learnt reaction.

113782.q: A dog only gets food after a high note, never after a low note. How does it react after a while?
a: It only drools at the high note
It drools equally at both notes
It no longer drools at either note
It only drools at the low note
113782.e: The dog learns to tell similar notes apart. Only the note that is followed by food sets off the reaction.
113782.m: Animals can learn to tell similar stimuli apart.

113783.q: What did the researcher John B. Watson want to show with experiments such as “Little Albert”?
a: That feelings such as fear can be learnt
That fear is inborn and cannot be changed
113783.e: Watson showed that fear can also be learnt through conditioning. He mainly studied behaviour that can be observed.
113783.m: Feelings such as fear can also be learnt.

113784.q: After an upset stomach, you feel disgusted for a long time by the food you ate beforehand. What is this learnt effect called?
113784.e: Even a single link between food and feeling sick can create a strong dislike. This is a special form of classical conditioning.
113784.m: A taste aversion can develop after just one bad experience.

113785.q: Which country did the researcher Ivan Pavlov come from?
113785.e: Ivan Petrovich Pavlov was a Russian physiologist. He lived from 1849 to 1936.
113785.m: Ivan Pavlov was a Russian researcher.

113786.q: What did Pavlov receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for in 1904?
a: For discovering the circulation of the blood
113786.e: Pavlov received the Nobel Prize for his work on the digestive glands. His famous learning experiments only grew out of this research.
113786.m: Pavlov received the Nobel Prize for research on digestion.

113787.q: Which bodily reaction of the dogs did Pavlov measure in his experiments?
113787.e: Pavlov collected and measured the liquid from the dogs' salivary glands. This let him find out exactly when and how strongly they reacted.
113787.m: Pavlov measured the flow of saliva in his dogs.

113788.q: With which animals did Ivan Pavlov carry out his famous learning experiments?
113788.e: Pavlov did research with dogs in St Petersburg for decades. He showed that they learn to link a signal with food.
113788.m: Pavlov did his learning experiments with dogs.

113789.q: In stories about Pavlov's experiment, which stimulus is usually linked with the food?
113789.e: In many accounts, a bell rings before the food. Pavlov himself also used a metronome and buzzers, among other things.
113789.m: With Pavlov's dog, a sound announces the food.

113790.q: What did Pavlov call the learnt reaction of his dogs?
113790.e: A conditioned reflex only develops through experience. Inborn reflexes such as blinking, on the other hand, do not need to be learnt.
113790.m: A conditioned reflex develops through experience.

113791.q: What do people mean when they say someone reacts “like Pavlov's dog”?
a: They react automatically to a learnt signal
113791.e: The expression describes a reaction that follows a familiar signal without thinking. One example is reaching for your mobile phone when it rings.

113792.q: When must the sound be heard so that the dog learns the link to the food best?
a: Long after the food has been eaten
113792.e: The signal has to announce the food, so it must come just before it. Then the dog learns fastest that the two belong together.
113792.m: A signal is learnt best when it comes shortly before the event.

113793.q: What is motivation called that comes from enjoying the activity itself?
113793.e: If you do something because it is fun or interesting, you are intrinsically motivated. The motivation comes from inside.

113794.q: A child only learns in order to get a reward. What is this kind of motivation called?
113794.e: With this motivation, the incentive comes from outside, for example through marks, praise or money. The activity itself is not the main thing.

113795.q: Which needs form the bottom level of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
a: Basic physical needs such as food and sleep
113795.e: First, hunger, thirst and the need for sleep must be satisfied. According to this theory, only then do higher needs become important.
113795.m: At the bottom of the hierarchy of needs are the basic physical needs.

113798.q: What is the state called in which you are completely absorbed in an activity and forget the time?
113798.e: The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described flow. It often happens when a task is neither too easy nor too hard.
113798.m: In flow, you are completely absorbed in an activity.

113799.q: What can happen if you are regularly rewarded for an activity that you enjoy doing anyway?
a: Your enjoyment of the activity can drop
You immediately get better at it
You no longer need any sleep
113799.e: Experiments show that rewards can push aside your own desire to do something. Experts call this the overjustification effect.
113799.m: Rewards can reduce the enjoyment of something.

113800.q: According to goal-setting theory, which goals boost performance the most?
a: Vague goals such as “Do your best”
113800.e: Edwin Locke and Gary Latham found that clear, demanding goals lead to better performance than unclear ones. It is important that you accept the goal.
113800.m: Clear and demanding goals spur you on.

113801.q: How many basic emotions did Paul Ekman originally name?
113801.e: Ekman named joy, sadness, fear and anger, among others. These basic feelings show in typical facial expressions.
113801.m: Ekman originally described six basic feelings.

113802.q: What does the amygdala in the brain do?
a: It raises the alarm when there is danger
113802.e: The amygdala judges in a flash whether something is dangerous. It can trigger a fear reaction even before we think.
113802.m: The amygdala raises the alarm when there is danger.

113803.q: Which naturalist wrote a book in 1872 about the expression of the emotions in humans and animals?
113803.e: Darwin compared the facial expressions of humans and animals. He thought that many ways of expressing feelings are inborn.
113803.m: Darwin also studied how feelings become visible.

113804.q: What did Paul Ekman's research in Papua New Guinea show?
a: Basic feelings are shown in similar ways on faces all over the world
Every people has completely different facial expressions
113804.e: Ekman showed photos of faces to people who had no contact with Western media. They recognised the basic feelings in a similar way to people in other countries.
113804.m: Basic feelings are recognised in similar ways in all cultures.

113805.q: Which system in the brain do areas that are strongly involved in feelings belong to?
113805.e: The limbic system lies deep in the brain. It processes feelings and is closely linked with memory.

113806.q: How did the psychologist Robert Plutchik arrange the emotions in his “wheel of emotions”?
a: Similar ones next to each other, opposites facing each other
By how loudly they are expressed
113806.e: Robert Plutchik arranged eight basic emotions in a circle. Joy, for example, is opposite sadness.
113806.m: Plutchik arranged emotions in a wheel.

113807.q: What is the ability to recognise your own and other people's feelings and handle them well called?
113807.e: The term became very well known in the 1990s through Daniel Goleman. It includes self-awareness and empathy.
113807.m: Emotional intelligence helps you deal with feelings.

113808.q: Which feeling is one of Ekman's basic emotions?
113808.e: All over the world, disgust shows in a typical wrinkling of the nose. Feelings such as jealousy or pride are seen as more complex.
113808.m: Disgust is a basic feeling with a typical facial expression.

113809.q: In a famous experiment, people had to say which line was the same length as another. The others in the group deliberately gave wrong answers. What did many of the test subjects do?
a: They gave the wrong answer too
They left the room at once
They did not notice the wrong answers
They could not see the lines
113809.e: Even though the task was very easy, many went along with the wrong majority. In this way, the psychologist Solomon Asch showed how strong group pressure is.
113809.m: Many people go along with a majority, even when it is wrong.

a: You take part in a dare because all your friends are doing it
You eat because you are hungry
You sleep because you are tired
You put on a jacket because it is cold
113810.e: With group pressure, you do something not because you want to, but because you want to belong.
113810.m: Group pressure means doing something only because the others are doing it.

113811.q: What helps you resist group pressure?
a: Saying no clearly and sticking to your own opinion
Always doing what the majority wants
113811.e: If you know what you want and say so calmly, you are less easily influenced. It also helps to have a friend who thinks the same way.
113811.m: If you stick to your opinion, you resist group pressure better.

113812.q: What do you call it when someone adapts their opinion or behaviour to a group?
113812.e: Conformity means adapting to the norms or opinions of a group. Group pressure can make it stronger.
113812.m: Conformity is adapting to a group.

113813.q: In the Asch experiment, what happened when one other person in the group also gave the right answer?
a: Going along with the majority dropped sharply
The experiment had to be stopped
Going along with the majority rose sharply
113813.e: Just one ally made it much easier to disagree with the majority. People no longer felt alone.
113813.m: A single ally helps you resist group pressure.

113814.q: What is the term for pressure from people of your own age?
113814.e: “Peers” are people of the same age, such as friends or classmates. Their influence is especially strong in the teenage years.
113814.m: Peer pressure is pressure from people your own age.

113815.q: What do you call it when a group makes bad decisions because it wants to agree?
113815.e: Irving Janis described groupthink. Critical opinions are held back so that harmony is kept.
113815.m: In groupthink, critical voices are held back.

113816.q: What is the effect called where people are less likely to help in an emergency when many others are watching?
113816.e: Everyone thinks that someone else will help. So nobody feels responsible.
113816.m: With the bystander effect, everyone relies on the others.

113817.q: What do you call a simplified, generalised idea about a whole group of people?
113817.e: A stereotype gives all members of a group the same characteristics. This is not fair to the individual people.
113817.m: A stereotype generalises about a whole group.

113819.q: According to the contact hypothesis, what can reduce prejudice between groups?
a: Positive contact on an equal footing
113819.e: When people from different groups meet as equals and work together, prejudice often decreases. This idea goes back to Gordon Allport.
113819.m: Meeting as equals breaks down prejudice.

113820.q: A teacher divided her class by eye colour and favoured one group. What did the children learn from this?
a: How to work out eye colour
That brown eyes make you cleverer
113820.e: The American teacher Jane Elliott did this exercise in 1968. The children experienced for themselves how it feels to be treated badly because of a random feature.
113820.m: A random feature can lead to discrimination.

113821.q: What is the tendency called to pay attention mainly to information that confirms your own opinion?
113821.e: With confirmation bias, we mainly notice what fits our opinion and overlook examples that go against it. This can make prejudices stick.
113821.m: Confirmation bias makes us see mainly information that fits.

113822.q: In Muzafer Sherif's summer camp experiment, what reduced the hostility between two groups?
113822.e: The young people had to solve tasks that could only be managed together. After that, quarrelling and putting each other down decreased.

113823.q: What do you call the tendency to favour your own group over other groups?
113823.e: Even when people are put into groups at random, they often favour their own. This can strengthen prejudice against others.
113823.m: People often favour their own group.

113824.q: Apart from a vase, what can you see in the ambiguous picture known as the “Rubin vase”?
113824.e: The white area in the middle is a vase, and the dark edges on the left and right are two faces looking at each other. Depending on how you look, you see one or the other.
113824.m: The Rubin vase shows a vase or two faces.

113825.q: What is special about an ambiguous picture?
a: You can see it in two ways
You can only see it in the dark
113825.e: With an ambiguous picture, your perception jumps back and forth between two interpretations. But you cannot see both pictures at the same time.
113825.m: An ambiguous picture can be seen in two ways.

113826.q: What is confusing about the Necker cube, a cube drawn with lines?
a: You cannot tell which side is at the front
It disappears when you look at it
113826.e: The Geneva researcher Louis Albert Necker described this cube in 1832. The view jumps back and forth: sometimes one face is at the front, sometimes the other.
113826.m: With the Necker cube, the front side jumps back and forth.

113827.q: Which two animals are shown in the well-known ambiguous picture described by Joseph Jastrow in 1899?
113827.e: Depending on how you look, you see a duck's head with a beak or a rabbit's head with ears. The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein later made the picture even more famous.
113827.m: Jastrow's ambiguous picture hides a duck or a rabbit.

113828.q: Which two figures are shown in the ambiguous picture “My Wife and My Mother-in-Law”?
a: A young woman and an old woman
113828.e: What is the ear and chin of the young woman becomes the eye and nose of the old woman. Many people at first see only one of the two.
113828.m: The same picture can show a young or an old woman.

113829.q: What do you experience when you look at an ambiguous picture?
a: You see both interpretations in turn, but never at the same time
You always see both interpretations at the same time
The picture really changes its colours
The picture moves on the paper
113829.e: The brain chooses one interpretation at a time. At that moment the other one cannot be seen, even if you know it is there.
113829.m: With an ambiguous picture, the brain switches between two interpretations.

113830.q: Which distinction in perception does the Rubin vase use?
113830.e: The brain splits a picture into a figure in the foreground and a background. In the Rubin vase, both parts can be the figure.

113831.q: How can you see the Schröder staircase?
a: Once from above and once from below
113831.e: You can see the drawn staircase as a normal staircase from above or as an upside-down staircase from below. The view suddenly flips.
113831.m: The Schröder staircase flips between two views.

113832.q: What does the abbreviation REM in REM sleep stand for?
113832.e: In REM sleep, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the eyelids. That is where the name comes from.
113832.m: In REM sleep, the eyes move quickly.

113833.q: What did researchers observe in sleeping people in the 1950s?
a: That the brain switches off completely
113833.e: In 1953 in Chicago, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman discovered REM sleep with its rapid eye movements. This was the start of modern sleep research.
113833.m: REM sleep was discovered in the 1950s.

113834.q: In which phase of sleep do people have especially vivid dreams?
113834.e: People woken from REM sleep especially often report vivid dreams. But people also dream in other phases.
113834.m: Vivid dreams happen mainly in REM sleep.

113835.q: Roughly how long does a sleep cycle last in an adult?
113835.e: A cycle of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep lasts about an hour and a half. You go through several of them each night.
113835.m: A sleep cycle lasts about an hour and a half.

113836.q: Which method is used in a sleep laboratory to measure brain waves?
113836.e: In electroencephalography, or EEG for short, electrodes are stuck onto the scalp. They record the electrical activity of the brain.
113836.m: Brain waves are measured with an EEG.

113837.q: Which hormone makes us tired in the evening and is produced in larger amounts in the dark?
113837.e: Melatonin is made in the pineal gland, mainly in the dark. Bright light in the evening can slow down its production.
113837.m: Melatonin is the hormone that makes you tired.

113838.q: How many hours of sleep a night do expert bodies recommend for teenagers aged 13 to 18?
113838.e: Teenagers need a lot of sleep because their bodies and brains are still developing. Expert bodies recommend 8 to 10 hours.
113838.m: Teenagers need about eight to ten hours of sleep.

113839.q: The Zurich researcher Alexander Borbély explained sleep with two processes. What are they?
a: Sleep pressure and the body clock
113839.e: The longer you are awake, the greater the sleep pressure. The body clock also decides when we get tired. The model from 1982 is still used today.
113839.m: Sleep pressure and the body clock control sleep together.

113840.q: What does the word “circadian” in circadian rhythm mean?
113840.e: The word comes from the Latin “circa diem”, meaning “about a day”. The body clock runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle.
113840.m: The body clock follows a rhythm of about one day.

113841.q: What do you call positive, motivating stress?
113841.e: Eustress motivates you and helps you perform, for example before a competition. Stress that weighs you down, on the other hand, is called distress.

113842.q: Which organs release stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline?
113842.e: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. Under strain, they release hormones into the blood that put the body on alert.
113842.m: The adrenal glands make stress hormones.

113843.q: What is the body's quick emergency response to a threat called?
113843.e: Walter Cannon described how the body prepares in a flash to fight or run away. This response already helped our ancestors to survive.
113843.m: In danger, the body prepares to fight or run away.

113844.q: What happens in the body during acute stress?
113844.e: During stress, the heart pumps faster to supply the muscles with blood. Digestion, on the other hand, is slowed down.
113844.m: During stress, the heart beats faster.

113845.q: At what level of tension does a test usually go best?
a: At a medium level of tension
Only when you are very tired
113845.e: A bit of tension makes you alert and focused, but too much blocks you. Experts call this link the Yerkes-Dodson law.
113845.m: A medium level of tension usually leads to the best performance.

113847.q: Which measure has been shown to help reduce stress?
a: Always being on your mobile phone
113847.e: Sport and exercise help to break down stress hormones and improve your mood. Getting enough sleep and taking breaks are also important.

113848.q: What can happen if stress lasts for a very long time?
a: The heart beats slower and slower
113848.e: With constant stress, the body's strength is used up at some point. The researcher Hans Selye called this the exhaustion stage.
113848.m: Constant stress can lead to exhaustion.

113849.q: Which country did the child researcher Jean Piaget come from?
113849.e: Jean Piaget was born in Neuchâtel in 1896 and did research in Geneva for a long time. He became one of the best-known developmental psychologists in the world.
113849.m: Jean Piaget was a Swiss researcher.

113853.q: A child thinks there is more water in a tall, narrow glass than there was before in the wide glass. What has the child not yet understood?
113853.e: The amount of water stays the same, even if it looks different. But younger children are fooled by the height of the water.
113853.m: An amount stays the same, even if its shape changes.

113854.q: According to Piaget, what can young people do in the formal operational stage, from about 11 or 12 years old?
a: Grasp things for the first time
Speak words for the first time
Recognise objects for the first time
113854.e: In this stage, you can think about thoughts, make hypotheses and test them logically. You no longer depend on things you can see and touch.
113854.m: Young people learn to think abstractly.

113855.q: What did Jean Piaget mainly study?
113855.e: Piaget watched children closely and gave them small tasks. That is how he found out how their thinking develops step by step.
113855.m: Piaget studied how children learn to think.

113856.q: What did Piaget's three mountains experiment show in younger children?
a: They find it hard to see things from someone else's point of view
113856.e: The children had to say how a doll would see the mountain landscape from another side. Younger children usually described their own view. Piaget called this egocentrism.
113856.m: Younger children often start from their own point of view.

113857.q: What did Piaget already study scientifically as a teenager?
113857.e: As a teenager, Piaget was already publishing articles about snails and other molluscs. Later he earned a doctorate in natural sciences.
113857.m: Piaget started out as a young naturalist.

113858.q: Which three parts make up the so-called habit loop?
113858.e: A cue starts a well-practised behaviour, which is followed by a reward. Through repetition, this loop becomes more and more automatic.
113858.m: Habits form from a cue, a routine and a reward.

113859.q: In a study by Phillippa Lally in 2009, how long did it take on average for a new behaviour to become a habit?
113859.e: On average it took about two months, but there were big differences depending on the person and the behaviour. Some needed much less time, others much longer.
113859.m: A new habit often takes about two months.

113860.e: Well-practised routines are stored deep in the brain. This means habits can run almost without thinking.
113860.m: Habits are stored in the brain.

113861.q: You often hear that a new habit forms in exactly 21 days. Is that true?
a: No, it is an inaccurate rule of thumb
113861.e: The 21-day rule is not backed up by science. How long it takes depends on the person and the behaviour.
113861.m: The 21-day rule for habits is not scientifically proven.

113862.q: Why do you stop hearing the ticking of a clock after a while?
a: The brain filters out sounds that stay the same
113862.e: The brain mainly pays attention to new things. Over time, it filters out a harmless stimulus that stays the same.
113862.m: Harmless stimuli that stay the same are filtered out over time.

113863.q: Which plan helps most to really practise every day?
a: “When I get home from school, I will practise for ten minutes.”
“I will practise when I feel like it.”
113863.e: An if-then plan links the new behaviour to a fixed situation. This makes you less likely to forget it.
113863.m: If-then plans help you stick to your intentions.

113864.q: Why do habits take the load off the brain?
a: They need a lot of concentration
They have to be learnt again every time
113864.e: When you brush your teeth or ride a bike, you do not have to think about every step. This leaves attention free for new things.

113865.q: Which strategy often helps you get rid of an unwanted habit?
a: Changing the cue in your surroundings
113865.e: If, for example, you put your mobile phone in another room while studying, you come across the cue less often. This makes it easier to drop the old behaviour.
113865.m: If you remove the cue, it is easier to break a habit.

a: Natural substances from plants that are often poisonous
113866.e: Alkaloids are made mainly by plants. Many have a strong effect on the body, for example caffeine or nicotine.
113866.m: Alkaloids are strong, often poisonous plant substances.

113867.q: Which poisonous alkaloid forms in green patches on potatoes?
113867.e: Green patches and sprouts on potatoes contain solanine. That is why you cut them away generously before cooking.
113867.m: Green patches on potatoes contain poisonous solanine.

113868.q: Which well-known alkaloid is found in coffee beans?
113868.e: Caffeine is an alkaloid that keeps you awake. It is also found in tea leaves, for example.
113868.m: The caffeine in coffee is also an alkaloid.

113869.q: Which alkaloid comes from the tobacco plant?
113869.e: The tobacco plant makes nicotine in its leaves. For insects it is a strong poison.
113869.m: Nicotine is the poisonous alkaloid of the tobacco plant.

113870.q: What do most alkaloids taste like?
113870.e: Most alkaloids taste bitter. The bitter taste often warns animals and people of something poisonous.
113870.m: Many plant poisons taste bitter and so warn of danger.

113871.q: What are alkaloids probably for in the plant itself?
a: Protection from animals that eat them
113871.e: Plants cannot run away. Poisonous and bitter substances such as alkaloids stop many animals from eating them.
113871.m: Plants protect themselves with alkaloids from animals that want to eat them.

113872.q: Which plant is the alkaloid morphine obtained from?
113872.e: Morphine comes from the milky sap of the opium poppy. It is a strong painkiller that only doctors may prescribe.
113872.m: The painkiller morphine is obtained from the opium poppy.

113873.q: Why must you not give chocolate to dogs?
a: It contains a substance that is poisonous to dogs
It makes dogs tired at once
113873.e: Cocoa contains the alkaloid theobromine. People break it down quickly, but dogs only very slowly, so it can poison them.

113874.q: Which bitter alkaloid from the bark of the cinchona tree helped against malaria?
113874.e: Quinine is obtained from the bark of the cinchona tree. For a long time it was the most important remedy against malaria, and it gives tonic water its bitter taste.
113874.m: Quinine from cinchona bark was long the most important malaria remedy.

113875.q: Which poisonous plant with shiny black berries contains the poison atropine?
113875.e: The scientific name of deadly nightshade is Atropa belladonna. The poison atropine gets its name from it.
113875.m: Deadly nightshade contains the poison atropine.

113876.e: Atropine is a strong poison found in deadly nightshade and other members of the nightshade family.

113877.q: Which part of the body does the poison atropine mainly affect?
113877.e: Atropine disrupts the passing on of signals in the nervous system. This changes things like the heartbeat, saliva and pupils.
113877.m: Atropine acts on the nervous system.

113878.q: Which plant family does deadly nightshade belong to?
113878.e: Like the potato, deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family. Many plants in this family contain poisons.
113878.m: Deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family.

113879.q: Why should you never eat unknown berries in the forest?
a: They could be poisonous like deadly nightshade
They make you tired at once
113879.e: Some berries, such as deadly nightshade, are deadly even in small amounts. That is why you only eat berries you know for certain.

113880.q: What should you do if someone has eaten deadly nightshade berries?
a: Call Tox Info on 145 or the emergency number at once
Get them to drink lots of milk
113880.e: Deadly nightshade poisoning is life-threatening. Tox Info Suisse on 145 and the emergency number 144 can help straight away.
113880.m: In case of poisoning, call 145 or 144 at once.

113881.q: Can a poison like atropine also be useful as a medicine?
a: Yes, in a small, exact dose
113881.e: In small, exactly measured amounts, doctors use atropine as a medicine, for example as an antidote to nerve poisons. The dose makes the poison.
113881.m: The dose decides whether a substance is poisonous or healing.

113882.q: What does “belladonna”, the species name of deadly nightshade, mean in Italian?
113882.e: In the past, women dripped deadly nightshade juice into their eyes. This made their pupils large, which was seen as beautiful. But it was dangerous.

113883.q: Besides deadly nightshade, which of these plants also contains atropine?
113883.e: The thorn apple is also a member of the nightshade family and contains poisons similar to deadly nightshade. Its seeds are especially poisonous.
113883.m: The thorn apple contains poisons similar to deadly nightshade.

113884.q: In which parts of monkshood is the poison especially concentrated?
a: In the hairs on the stem
113884.e: Aconitine is in all parts of the plant. But the root tubers and the seeds contain the most.
113884.m: In monkshood, the roots and seeds are especially poisonous.

113885.q: What amount of aconitine can already be deadly for an adult?
113885.e: Just about 5 milligrams of pure aconitine can kill an adult. That is a tiny amount, much less than a gram.
113885.m: Just a few milligrams of aconitine are life-threatening.

113886.q: Which Alpine plant contains the strong poison aconitine?
113886.e: Monkshood is considered the most poisonous plant in Europe. Its poison is called aconitine.

113887.q: What should you do if you see monkshood while hiking?
a: Do not pick it and do not touch it
113887.e: The poison of monkshood can even be taken in through the skin. So it is best to leave the plant where it is.

113888.q: Which first sign is typical of aconitine poisoning?
113888.e: Aconitine disrupts the nerves. First the mouth and skin tingle, and later the skin in these places goes numb.
113888.m: Monkshood poisoning often starts with tingling and numbness.

113889.q: Which plant family does monkshood belong to?
113889.e: Monkshood belongs to the buttercup family. There are many poisonous species in this family, including the buttercup itself.
113889.m: Monkshood belongs to the buttercup family.

113890.q: Where does the German name of monkshood, “Eisenhut” (iron hat), come from?
a: Its flower looks like a helmet
It only grows on iron ore
Its stems are as hard as iron
113890.e: The top petal arches like a knight's helmet, which used to be called an iron hat. That is where the name comes from. The English name monkshood compares it to a monk's hood.
113890.m: The monkshood flower looks like a helmet.

113891.q: Which organ can aconitine disrupt in a life-threatening way?
113891.e: Aconitine throws the heart rhythm into confusion and paralyses breathing. A person can die from this.
113891.m: Aconitine can throw the heart out of rhythm.

113892.q: Which plant contains the poison colchicine?
113892.e: The autumn crocus contains colchicine in all its parts. The seeds and the bulb are especially poisonous.
113892.m: The poison of the autumn crocus is called colchicine.

113893.q: Which edible plant are the poisonous leaves of the autumn crocus often confused with in spring?
113893.e: The autumn crocus puts out its leaves in spring, when wild garlic is also being gathered. Its leaves contain the dangerous poison colchicine.
113893.m: The autumn crocus can be confused with wild garlic.

113894.q: Where is the ovary of the autumn crocus while it flowers in autumn?
a: At the top of the flower
113894.e: During flowering, the ovary stays protected deep in the ground. Only the following spring does the seed capsule grow upwards with the leaves.
113894.m: In the autumn crocus, the ovary stays in the ground while it flowers.

113895.q: What does colchicine block in the cells?
113895.e: Colchicine stops cells from dividing properly. That is why it mainly harms tissues that renew themselves quickly, such as the gut.
113895.m: Colchicine is a poison that stops cells dividing.

113896.q: What is true of colchicine, the poison of the autumn crocus?
a: In tiny amounts it is used as a medicine
It is used as a sweetener
113896.e: In very small, exactly measured amounts, colchicine is used for example against gout. But just a little more can be deadly.
113896.m: Colchicine is poisonous but helps as a medicine in tiny amounts.

113897.q: What is typical of the course of colchicine poisoning?
a: The symptoms only begin after hours
You feel severe pain at once
The skin turns blue at once
113897.e: First symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhoea often only appear a few hours after eating. That is why the danger is easily underestimated.
113897.m: Autumn crocus poisoning often only shows after hours.

113899.q: Why is the autumn crocus dangerous for cows too when it is in the hay?
a: The poison remains when it dries
The plant becomes prickly in the hay
113899.e: On the pasture, animals usually avoid the plant. But in hay they recognise it less easily, and the colchicine stays poisonous even when dried.
113899.m: Dried autumn crocus in hay stays poisonous too.

113900.q: Which tree contains the poison taxine?
113900.e: The scientific name of the yew is Taxus. That is why its poison is called taxine.
113900.m: The yew is a poisonous conifer with the poison taxine.

113901.q: How old can a yew tree become?
113901.e: The yew grows very slowly and can reach an enormous age. Some yews are well over 1,000 years old.
113901.m: Yews can live for over 1,000 years.

113902.q: Which organ does taxine mainly affect?
113902.e: Taxine disrupts the heart rhythm. In severe poisoning the heart can stop.
113902.m: The yew's poison mainly attacks the heart.

113903.q: Why do not all yew trees bear red fruits?
a: There are male and female trees
Only old yews are poisonous enough
The fruits only grow in the shade
113903.e: The yew has separate male and female trees: male and female flowers grow on different trees. Only female yews form seeds with the red seed coat.
113903.m: Only female yews bear the red fruits.

113904.q: How do yew seeds often reach new places?
a: Birds eat the fruits and drop the seeds in their droppings
The wind carries the heavy seeds far away
Bees carry the seeds into their hive
The seeds float away on rivers
113904.e: Birds eat the sweet red seed coat. They pass out the hard seed undigested and so spread the yew.
113904.m: Birds spread the seeds of the yew.

113905.q: How do roe deer react to young yew shoots?
a: They die from them at once
113905.e: For roe deer the yew is far less dangerous than for horses. They like nibbling the young shoots, which harms young yews in the forest.
113905.m: Roe deer like eating young yew shoots.

113906.q: What does the yew do in winter?
113906.e: The yew is an evergreen conifer. That is why it often grows in gardens, parks and churchyards, in Switzerland too.
113906.m: The yew stays green even in winter.

113907.q: What is a substance from the bark of one kind of yew used for in medicine today?
113907.e: A substance that slows the growth of cancer cells was found in the bark of the Pacific yew. A cancer medicine was developed from it.
113907.m: A cancer medicine comes from the yew.

113908.q: Where in the potato is there the most solanine?
a: In and just under the skin
113908.e: The highest levels are in the skin, the layer below it and the eyes. Peeling and cutting away green patches greatly lowers the amount.
113908.m: Most solanine is in and under the potato skin.

113909.q: How should you store potatoes so that they form little solanine?
113909.e: Light and warmth make potatoes turn green and sprout. In the dark and cool, they form much less solanine.
113909.m: Store potatoes somewhere dark and cool.

113910.q: Which part of the potato plant is poisonous and must never be eaten?
113910.e: After flowering, the potato plant forms small green berries. They look like mini tomatoes but contain lots of solanine.
113910.m: The small green berries of the potato plant are poisonous.

113911.q: What happens to solanine when cooking?
113911.e: Solanine can withstand high temperatures. So cooking does not make green patches safe; you have to cut them away.
113911.m: Solanine is not destroyed by cooking.

113912.q: Which symptoms does too much solanine typically cause?
113912.e: Solanine irritates the stomach and gut. It causes tummy pain, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.
113912.m: Too much solanine causes tummy pain and vomiting.

113913.q: Where does solanine get its name from?
a: From the sun, sol in Latin
113913.e: The potato belongs to the genus Solanum, the nightshades. The poison is named after it.
113913.m: Solanine is named after the genus Solanum, which the potato belongs to.

113914.q: Which vegetable, when unripe and green, contains poisons similar to green potatoes?
113914.e: Like the potato, the tomato belongs to the nightshade family. Unripe tomatoes contain similar poisonous substances, which break down as they ripen.
113914.m: Unripe green tomatoes contain poisons similar to green potatoes.

113915.e: The potato plant makes solanine to protect itself from animals that eat it. There is especially a lot in green patches, sprouts and berries.
113915.m: Solanine is a poison made by the potato plant.

113916.q: Which very strong poison is found in the seeds of the castor oil plant?
113916.e: The seeds of the castor oil plant (Ricinus) contain ricin. It is one of the most poisonous natural substances.
113916.m: Castor oil plant seeds contain the very strong poison ricin.

113917.q: What does the Latin word “ricinus” mean?
113917.e: The spotted seeds look like ticks that have sucked themselves full. That is where the plant gets its name.
113917.m: Ricinus means tick, because the seeds look like ticks.

113918.q: Why is castor oil not poisonous, even though it is pressed from poisonous seeds?
a: The poison stays in the pressed residue
The oil is mixed with sugar
113918.e: Ricin does not dissolve in oil. It stays behind in the press cake, so the oil itself is not poisonous.
113918.m: When the seeds are pressed, the poison ricin stays in the residue and not in the oil.

113919.q: What was castor oil often used for as a home remedy in the past?
113919.e: Castor oil strongly stimulates the bowels. In the past it was often taken for constipation.
113919.m: Castor oil is a strong laxative.

113920.q: How can you easily recognise the castor oil plant in a garden?
a: By its large, hand-shaped, often red leaves
113920.e: The castor oil plant has large leaves lobed like a hand, often reddish in colour. That is why it is planted as an ornamental plant.
113920.m: The castor oil plant has large, hand-shaped leaves.

113921.q: How does ricin act in the body's cells?
a: It stops the production of proteins
113921.e: Ricin paralyses the ribosomes, which make proteins. Without new proteins, the cells die.
113921.m: Ricin stops cells from making proteins.

113922.q: Why is chewing castor oil seeds more dangerous than swallowing whole seeds?
a: Only the broken seed coat releases the poison
Chewed seeds get bigger in the mouth
Whole seeds contain no poison at all
113922.e: The hard seed coat partly holds back the poison. If the seed is chewed, the ricin gets into the body much more easily.
113922.m: Chewed castor oil seeds are especially dangerous.

113923.q: Where are you most likely to find the castor oil plant in Switzerland?
a: As an ornamental plant in gardens and parks
Growing wild in the high mountains
113923.e: The castor oil plant comes from warmer regions. In Switzerland it is planted as an ornamental plant because of its large, often reddish leaves.
113923.m: In Swiss gardens the castor oil plant grows as an ornamental plant.

113924.q: Which region does the oleander originally come from?
113924.e: The oleander grows wild in the Mediterranean region, often on riverbanks. In Switzerland it is usually kept in pots on balconies and terraces.
113924.m: The oleander comes from the Mediterranean.

113925.q: Which organ does oleander poison mainly affect?
113925.e: Oleander contains so-called cardiac glycosides. They disrupt the heartbeat.

113926.q: A small child has eaten oleander leaves. What should you do straight away?
a: Wait and see if anything happens
113926.e: Oleander is very poisonous. In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps around the clock on 145; in an emergency you call 144.
113926.m: In cases of poisoning, the number 145 helps.

113927.q: Which parts of the oleander are poisonous?
113927.e: The leaves, flowers, stems, seeds and sap are poisonous. Even the smoke when it is burnt can be harmful.
113927.m: All parts of the oleander are poisonous.

113928.q: Why does an oleander in Switzerland usually need protecting in winter?
a: It needs lots of fertiliser in winter
It only flowers in the dark
113928.e: The oleander comes from mild regions. In hard frost it freezes, so it is brought indoors to a bright, cool place.
113928.m: Oleander must be protected from hard frost.

113929.q: What is true of the oleander's leaves?
a: It sheds all its leaves in autumn
It has no leaves at all
113929.e: The oleander keeps its narrow, leathery leaves all year. This helps it survive well in the dry Mediterranean climate.
113929.m: The oleander is an evergreen shrub.

113930.q: What do oleander leaves look like?
113930.e: The oleander has narrow, long, leathery leaves. This means it loses little water in the dry Mediterranean climate.
113930.m: The oleander has narrow, leathery leaves.

113931.q: What should you do with the branches after pruning an oleander?
a: Not burn them and not feed them to animals
113931.e: Smoke and dried leaves are poisonous too. So cuttings belong neither on a fire nor with pets.
113931.m: You do not burn oleander branches or give them to animals.

113932.q: How do the flowers of the angel's trumpet hang on the plant?
a: Flat plates lie on the ground
113932.e: The large trumpet-shaped flowers hang downwards. On the related thorn apple, by contrast, they point upwards.
113932.m: Angel's trumpets have large, hanging trumpet-shaped flowers.

113933.q: Which continent do angel's trumpets come from?
113933.e: Angel's trumpets come from South America. In Switzerland they are popular potted plants.
113933.m: The angel's trumpet comes from South America.

113934.q: Which plant family does the angel's trumpet belong to?
113934.e: The angel's trumpet belongs to the nightshade family, like deadly nightshade and the potato. It contains poisons similar to those of deadly nightshade.
113934.m: The angel's trumpet is a member of the nightshade family.

113935.q: Which parts of the angel's trumpet are poisonous?
113935.e: All parts of the angel's trumpet contain poisons such as scopolamine and atropine. These substances confuse the senses and strain the heart.
113935.m: The whole angel's trumpet is poisonous.

113936.q: Why is it dangerous to use angel's trumpets as a drug?
a: The amount of poison is almost impossible to judge
The plant has no effect at all
It is only harmful to animals
113936.e: The amount of poison varies greatly from plant to plant. It causes confusion, hallucinations and a racing heart, which can be fatal.
113936.m: Using angel's trumpets as a drug is life-threatening.

113937.q: When do angel's trumpet flowers smell strongest?
a: In the evening and at night
113937.e: The flowers give off a strong scent mainly in the evening. In their homeland this attracts pollinators that are active at night.
113937.m: Angel's trumpets smell especially strong in the evening.

113938.q: What is true of angel's trumpet species in the wild?
a: They are considered extinct in the wild
They are very common in the Alps
They only live in the sea
113938.e: All species are considered extinct in the wild. They only survive because people plant them.
113938.m: Today angel's trumpets are found almost only in gardens.

113939.q: What growth form does the angel's trumpet have?
113939.e: Angel's trumpets grow as woody shrubs or small trees. In pots they often grow more than two metres tall.
113939.m: The angel's trumpet grows as a shrub or small tree.

113940.q: Roughly when does ragwort (St James's wort) start to flower?
a: Around St James's Day at the end of July
113940.e: Its German name refers to St James's Day on 25 July. Around this time the yellow flowers are in full bloom.
113940.m: Ragwort flowers around St James's Day in July.

113941.q: What colour are the flowers of ragwort?
113941.e: The plant has many small yellow flower heads. It belongs to the daisy family.

113942.q: For which animals is ragwort especially dangerous?
a: For horses and cattle in pastures
113942.e: Ragwort contains poisonous substances called pyrrolizidine alkaloids. If horses or cattle eat it again and again, their liver is damaged.
113942.m: Ragwort is poisonous to grazing animals.

113943.q: Which organ do the poisons in ragwort mainly damage?
113943.e: The poisons gradually destroy the liver. Because the damage builds up, even small amounts are harmful over a long time.

113944.q: Why is ragwort in hay especially dangerous for horses and cattle?
a: In hay the warning bitter taste is missing
In hay the plant becomes sweeter and bigger
In hay the plant grows spines
In hay the poison multiplies greatly
113944.e: Animals often avoid fresh plants because of their bitter taste. When dried they notice this less, but the poison remains.
113944.m: Animals eat the poisonous plant in hay because it tastes less bitter there.

113945.q: The black and yellow striped caterpillar of the cinnabar moth eats poisonous ragwort. What happens as a result?
a: It becomes poisonous to birds itself
113945.e: The caterpillars store the plant's poison in their bodies. Their warning colours show birds that they are not good to eat.
113945.m: The cinnabar moth caterpillar eats ragwort and becomes poisonous itself.

113946.q: Why is the plant called “groundsel” in German, meaning “old man's herb”?
a: The white seed hairs look like an old man's hair
Only old people are allowed to pick it
It lives for very many years
It grows outside old people's homes
113946.e: After flowering, the seeds carry tufts of white hair. They look like the white hair of an old man.
113946.m: The white seed hairs gave the plant its German name.

113947.q: How are the seeds of ragwort spread?
113947.e: The seeds have fine little hairy parachutes like dandelions. With these they fly far on the wind, for example along roadsides.
113947.m: The wind spreads the seeds of ragwort.

113948.q: Which of these vegetables is wild garlic most closely related to?
113948.e: Wild garlic belongs to the onion genus, like chives, onions and garlic. That is why it has a similar taste.
113948.m: Wild garlic is a relative of chives and onions.

113949.q: What kind of substances give wild garlic its typical smell?
113949.e: When the leaves are crushed, substances containing sulphur are produced. They are responsible for the sharp, spicy smell.
113949.m: The smell of wild garlic comes from sulphur compounds.

113950.q: Why is the smell test unreliable when picking wild garlic?
a: The garlic smell sticks to your hands
Wild garlic has no smell at all
The smell can only be noticed at night
113950.e: After a few leaves, your fingers themselves smell of garlic. Then you can no longer smell the difference with a wrong leaf.
113950.m: When picking wild garlic, check each leaf separately, because your hands smell of garlic.

113951.q: What does wild garlic grow from again every spring?
a: From a bulb in the ground
From the branches of a shrub
113951.e: Wild garlic has a slender bulb in the ground. It stores nutrients there for the next spring.
113951.m: Wild garlic grows every year from a bulb in the ground.

113952.q: How do the leaves of wild garlic grow?
a: Each leaf has its own stalk coming out of the ground
Two leaves wrap around each other at the base
Many leaves sit without stalks in a rosette
The leaves grow on a tall stem
113952.e: With wild garlic, each leaf comes out of the ground separately on its own stalk. This helps to tell it apart from lily of the valley and autumn crocus.
113952.m: Each wild garlic leaf grows separately on its own stalk.

113953.q: What happens to wild garlic leaves a few months after they appear?
113953.e: Two to three months after they appear, the leaves turn yellow as the ground warms up. In summer there is hardly anything of the wild garlic to be seen above ground.
113953.m: In summer the wild garlic leaves disappear again.

113954.q: Where does wild garlic prefer to grow?
113954.e: Wild garlic likes shady, damp deciduous woods and floodplains. There it often forms large carpets.
113954.m: Wild garlic grows in damp deciduous woods.

113955.q: What do wild garlic flowers look like?
a: White little stars in a cluster
113955.e: Many small white star-shaped flowers sit together at the top of a stem. They flower in spring in the woods.
113955.m: Wild garlic has white star-shaped flowers in a cluster.

113956.q: What is the safest rule when picking wild plants such as wild garlic?
a: Only pick what you know for certain
Only take leaves at the edge of the wood
113956.e: Many poisonous plants look like edible plants. If you are unsure, leave the plant where it is.
113956.m: Only eat plants that you recognise with complete certainty.

113957.q: Who answers the calls at Tox Info Suisse?
113957.e: At Tox Info Suisse, doctors and other medical specialists give advice. The advice is free.
113957.m: At Tox Info Suisse, medical specialists give advice.

113958.q: Which short number do you dial in Switzerland in a case of poisoning to reach Tox Info Suisse?
113958.e: In Switzerland you can reach Tox Info Suisse around the clock on 145. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade. If someone is unconscious, you dial 144 straight away.
113958.m: In cases of poisoning, Tox Info Suisse helps on 145.

113959.q: Who can contact Tox Info Suisse?
a: Members of the public and specialists
113959.e: Tox Info Suisse advises members of the public as well as doctors, hospitals and companies. Anyone can get in touch about poisoning.
113959.m: Anyone can contact Tox Info Suisse about poisoning.

113960.q: When can you reach Tox Info Suisse?
113960.e: Tox Info Suisse can be reached day and night, including public holidays, on 145. The centre has existed since 1966.
113960.m: Tox Info Suisse helps around the clock.

113961.q: About how many enquiries did Tox Info Suisse receive in 2025?
113961.e: At the beginning there were around 2,000 enquiries a year. In 2025 there were 44,736 consultations, which is more than 40,000.
113961.m: Tox Info Suisse answers more than 40,000 enquiries every year.

113962.q: Which group accounts for about 40 per cent of enquiries to Tox Info Suisse?
113962.e: Small children put lots of things in their mouths. That is why around 40 per cent of enquiries concern children under five.
113962.m: Many cases of poisoning involve small children.

113963.q: What should you NOT do after someone has swallowed a poisonous plant?
113963.e: Making someone vomit can cause extra harm. It is better to call 145 straight away and follow the instructions.
113963.m: In a case of poisoning, do not make anyone vomit; call 145 instead.

113964.q: Why should you keep a piece of the plant after plant poisoning?
a: So that specialists can identify it
So that you can plant it later
So that it can act as an antidote
So that it does not wilt
113964.e: If it is known which plant was eaten, the danger can be judged better. That is why you show a piece or a photo of it.
113964.m: A piece of the plant helps to judge the poisoning correctly.

113965.q: What does Tox Info Suisse help with?
113965.e: Tox Info Suisse gives advice around the clock on 145 when someone has swallowed or touched something poisonous.
113965.m: Tox Info Suisse helps with poisoning, phone 145.

113966.q: What is the long extension of a nerve cell that passes on signals called?
113966.e: The axon carries the electrical signal away from the cell body to the next cell. It can be very long.
113966.m: The axon carries signals away from the nerve cell.

113967.q: What do the branched dendrites of a nerve cell do?
a: They receive signals from other cells
They store fat for the winter
113967.e: Dendrites are like antennae. They pick up signals from other nerve cells and pass them to the cell body.
113967.m: Dendrites are the antennae of the nerve cell.

113968.q: Roughly how many nerve cells does the human brain have?
113968.e: Researchers have estimated the number of nerve cells in the brain at about 86 billion. That is about ten times more than the number of people living on Earth.
113968.m: Our brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.

113969.q: What is the myelin sheath around many axons for?
a: It speeds up the passing on of signals
113969.e: The myelin sheath insulates the axon like the covering of a cable. This makes the signals jump along faster.
113969.m: Myelin insulates nerve fibres and makes signals travel faster.

113971.q: How do nerve cells pass on information?
113971.e: Nerve cells produce tiny electrical signals that travel through the body very quickly. That is how the message “hot” gets from your hand to your brain, for example.
113971.m: Nerve cells pass on information as electrical signals.

113972.q: What are the cells in the brain called that support and supply the nerve cells?
113972.e: Glial cells hold the nerve cells in place, supply them and in some cases form the myelin sheaths. Without them, the brain could not work.
113972.m: Glial cells are the helper cells of the nerve cells.

113973.q: What is the cord of nerve fibres in the back called that connects the brain and the body?
113973.e: The spinal cord runs protected inside the spine. It carries signals back and forth between the brain and the rest of the body.
113973.m: The spinal cord connects the brain and the body.

113974.q: Roughly how long can the longest nerve cells in humans be?
113974.e: Some nerve cells reach from the spinal cord to the toes. Their axon can therefore be about a metre long.
113974.m: The longest nerve cells reach from the back to the toes.

a: The point of contact between two nerve cells
A blood vessel in the brain
113975.e: At the synapse, a signal is passed from one nerve cell to the next or to a muscle cell. The word means “connection”.
113975.m: Synapses are the connection points between nerve cells.

113976.q: What are the messenger substances called that pass on signals at a synapse?
113976.e: Neurotransmitters are released by one cell and attach to the next cell. This passes the signal on.
113976.m: Neurotransmitters carry signals across the synapse.

113977.q: What is the tiny gap between two cells at a synapse called?
113977.e: There is a very narrow gap between the cells. The messenger substances have to cross it to pass the signal on.
113977.m: At the synapse, the messenger substances cross the synaptic cleft.

113978.q: Where are the messenger substances stored at the end of an axon?
113978.e: The messenger substances are kept in tiny bubbles called vesicles. When a signal arrives, the bubbles release their contents into the gap.
113978.m: Messenger substances are stored in small bubbles.

113979.q: What happens when a nerve releases a messenger substance at a skeletal muscle?
113979.e: At the junction between nerve and muscle, the messenger substance acetylcholine is released. This makes the muscle contract.
113979.m: A messenger substance makes the muscle contract.

113980.q: Which messenger substance is closely linked with the brain's reward system?
113980.e: Dopamine is released when something goes better than expected. It plays an important role in learning and motivation.
113980.m: Dopamine is part of the brain's reward system.

113981.q: What do inhibitory messenger substances do in the brain?
a: They slow down the activity of nerve cells
113981.e: Inhibitory messenger substances such as GABA slow nerve cells down. Excitatory messenger substances such as glutamate, on the other hand, stimulate them.
113981.m: Inhibitory messenger substances slow down nerve cells.

113982.q: What does the Greek word that “synapse” comes from mean?
113982.e: The British researcher Charles Sherrington introduced the term in 1897. It describes the point where two nerve cells connect.

113983.q: Roughly how many synapses are there in the human brain?
113983.e: Each nerve cell often has thousands of points of contact. In total, the number of synapses is estimated at about 100 trillion.
113983.m: There are about 100 trillion synapses in the brain.

113984.q: What is the bridge of nerves called that connects the two halves of the cerebrum?
113984.e: The corpus callosum consists of many millions of nerve fibres. The two halves of the brain exchange information through it.
113984.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

113985.q: Why is the surface of the cerebrum so heavily folded?
a: So that more cortex fits into the skull
So that the brain is lighter
So that less blood flows into it
So that the brain stays cooler
113985.e: The folds make the area of the cerebral cortex much larger. Even so, it still fits into the limited space of the skull.
113985.m: The folds increase the surface of the cerebral cortex.

113986.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum are visual impressions mainly processed?
113986.e: The visual cortex is in the occipital lobe, right at the back of the head. The signals from the eyes go there.
113986.m: We see with the back part of the cerebrum.

113987.q: Which lobe of the cerebrum mainly processes the skin's sense of touch?
113987.e: The centre for body sensations is in the parietal lobe. Signals of touch, pressure and temperature from the skin arrive there.
113987.m: The sense of touch is processed in the parietal lobe.

113988.q: Which half of the cerebrum controls the movements of the right side of the body?
113988.e: The nerve pathways cross over on their way to the body. That is why the left half of the brain controls the right side of the body and the other way round.
113988.m: The left half of the brain controls the right side of the body.

113989.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum are important areas for planning and making decisions?
113989.e: The frontal lobe is right behind the forehead. It is important for planning, making decisions and controlling your own behaviour.
113989.m: The frontal lobe helps us plan and make decisions.

113990.q: In which part of the brain do thinking, learning and remembering mainly happen?
113990.e: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain. Its cortex processes sensory impressions, and this is where we think, learn and remember.
113990.m: We think and learn in the cerebrum.

113991.q: What is the folded outer layer of the cerebrum with very many nerve cells called?
113991.e: The cerebral cortex is only a few millimetres thick but contains billions of nerve cells. Because of its colour, it is also called grey matter.
113991.m: The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of the cerebrum.

113992.q: In which lobe of the cerebrum is the hearing centre?
113992.e: The auditory cortex is in the temporal lobe, at the side of the head, roughly level with the ears. Sounds and speech are processed there.
113992.m: The hearing centre is in the temporal lobe.

113993.q: What is the main job of the cerebellum?
113993.e: The cerebellum makes sure that movements are smooth and precise. It also helps you keep your balance.
113993.m: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

113994.q: Which part of the brain contains more than half of all nerve cells?
113994.e: The cerebellum is small, but tightly packed. It contains most of all the nerve cells in the brain.
113994.m: The small cerebellum contains most of the nerve cells.

113995.q: Why do drunk people often walk unsteadily and sway?
113995.e: Alcohol affects the cerebellum. Then balance and coordination are disturbed.
113995.m: Alcohol disrupts the cerebellum and with it your balance.

113996.q: In which kind of learning is the cerebellum especially involved?
a: Practising movements such as riding a bike
113996.e: The cerebellum helps to fine-tune movements through practice. This is how riding a bike, for example, becomes automatic over time.
113996.m: The cerebellum helps you practise movements.

113997.q: What does the Latin name “cerebellum” mean?
113997.e: Cerebrum means brain, and cerebellum is the form meaning “small”. So the cerebellum is literally the “little brain”.

113998.q: Which sign is typical when the cerebellum is damaged?
a: Loss of the sense of smell
113998.e: When the cerebellum is damaged, movements look wobbly and imprecise. Experts call this ataxia.
113998.m: Damage to the cerebellum makes movements unsteady.

113999.q: Where in the head is the cerebellum?
a: At the back, under the cerebrum
At the front, behind the forehead
At the top, under the crown
At the side, behind the ears
113999.e: The cerebellum is at the back of the head, below the cerebrum. It is connected to the brainstem.
113999.m: The cerebellum is at the back of the head, under the cerebrum.

114000.q: Which vital function does the brainstem control?
114000.e: The brainstem contains centres that control breathing and circulation. They work completely without conscious thought.
114000.m: The brainstem controls breathing and heartbeat.

114001.q: Which parts belong to the brainstem?
a: Frontal lobe, corpus callosum and cerebellum
114001.e: The brainstem consists of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata. The medulla oblongata leads into the spinal cord.
114001.m: The midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata form the brainstem.

114002.q: What is the brainstem connected to at its lower end?
114002.e: The brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord. All the pathways between the brain and the body run through it.
114002.m: The brainstem connects the brain and the spinal cord.

114003.q: Which protective reflexes are controlled in the brainstem?
114003.e: Swallowing, coughing, sneezing and gagging are controlled by the brainstem. They protect the airways.
114003.m: The brainstem controls coughing and swallowing.

114004.q: Why is the brainstem considered the oldest part of the brain?
a: Very early vertebrates already had similar structures
It only forms in old age
114004.e: Fish, amphibians and reptiles also have a similar brainstem. It developed very early in the evolution of vertebrates.
114004.m: In evolutionary terms, the brainstem is the oldest part of the brain.

114005.q: Why is a serious injury to the brainstem so dangerous?
a: Vital functions such as breathing can fail
Afterwards you just cannot sing any more
It is not dangerous at all
114005.e: The brainstem controls breathing, heartbeat and circulation. If it fails, the body can no longer survive on its own.
114005.m: The brainstem is vital for life.

114006.q: What is a doctor checking when she shines a light into the eye and looks at the pupil?
a: Whether a reflex through the brainstem is working
Whether the corpus callosum is thick enough
114006.e: In light, the pupil gets smaller as a reflex. This pupil reflex runs through the brainstem.
114006.m: The pupil reflex shows whether the brainstem is working.

114007.q: Where in the head is the brainstem?
a: At the bottom of the brain, directly above the spinal cord
Right at the front behind the forehead
At the top under the skullcap
114007.e: The brainstem forms the lower part of the brain. It runs down into the neck, where it leads into the spinal cord.
114007.m: The brainstem is at the bottom of the brain.

a: The brain is made of plastic
The brain stays the same all your life
You can shape the brain like clay
114008.e: Neuroplasticity means that connections in the brain change through learning and experience. In this way, the brain is constantly adapting.
114008.m: Our brain changes when we learn.

114009.q: According to a well-known study, which part of the brain was larger in London taxi drivers?
114009.e: London taxi drivers learn thousands of streets by heart. In them, part of the hippocampus, which is important for spatial memory, was larger.
114009.m: Lots of practice at finding your way changes the hippocampus.

114010.q: What happens to the connection between two nerve cells that are often active at the same time?
114010.e: If two nerve cells are often active together, their connection gets stronger. That is why practice helps learning.
114010.m: Nerve cells that fire together wire together.

114011.q: What happens to rarely used connections in the brain?
a: They get weaker or are removed
They move into the spinal cord
114011.e: The brain removes connections that are hardly used. Connections that are used often, on the other hand, are strengthened.
114011.m: What we do not practise fades away in the brain.

114012.q: Why can people partly relearn lost abilities after a stroke?
a: Other brain areas take over tasks
114012.e: Thanks to neuroplasticity, healthy areas can take over the tasks of damaged areas. This takes a lot of training, for example in therapy.
114012.m: After a stroke, other brain areas can take over tasks.

114013.q: What did a study show in which adults practised juggling for three months?
a: Certain brain areas increased in volume
114013.e: After the training, certain areas of the cerebral cortex that see and process movement were larger. This shows that adults can change their brains too.
114013.m: Adults also change their brains when they practise something new.

114014.q: Which brain area is often also used by blind people when reading Braille?
114014.e: In blind people, the visual cortex is not needed for seeing. It can then help with feeling Braille.
114014.m: The brain can use unused areas for new tasks.

114015.q: At what stage of life can the brain change?
114015.e: In childhood the brain is especially easy to shape. But adults and older people can still learn new things too.
114015.m: We can learn new things throughout our lives.

a: The electrical activity of the brain
The blood pressure in the arms
114016.e: The EEG measures small changes in voltage caused by the activity of many nerve cells. The curves are called brainwaves.

114017.q: Since when has it been possible to record a person's brainwaves?
114017.e: The German doctor Hans Berger first recorded human brainwaves in Jena in 1924.
114017.m: The EEG in humans has existed for about 100 years.

114018.q: Where are the electrodes placed for a normal EEG?
a: On the soles of the feet
114018.e: For a normal EEG, electrodes are stuck or placed on the scalp, often using a cap. The measurement does not hurt.
114018.m: In an EEG, the electrodes sit on the scalp.

114019.q: What does the EEG show when someone who is awake relaxes and closes their eyes?
114019.e: When you are awake and relaxed with your eyes closed, even alpha waves appear. If you open your eyes, they usually become weaker.
114019.m: Relaxing with closed eyes shows up in the EEG.

114020.q: What do brainwaves look like in the EEG during deep sleep?
a: There are none, the brain is off
114020.e: In deep sleep the waves become very slow and large. They are called delta waves.
114020.m: In deep sleep the EEG shows slow, large waves.

114021.q: For which illness is the EEG especially helpful in diagnosis?
114021.e: In epilepsy, typical patterns often appear in the brainwaves. The EEG is therefore an important tool for diagnosis.

114022.q: In which unit do you state how fast brainwaves oscillate?
114022.e: Hertz states how many oscillations take place per second. Alpha waves oscillate about 8 to 13 times per second.
114022.m: The frequency of brainwaves is measured in hertz.

114023.q: What is the EEG used for in a sleep laboratory?
a: To determine the stages of sleep
114023.e: Brainwaves change depending on the stage of sleep. From the EEG, experts can tell whether someone is in light sleep, deep sleep or dream sleep.
114023.m: In a sleep lab, the EEG shows the stages of sleep.

114024.q: What is the correct order in a reflex arc?
a: Receptor, nerve, spinal cord, nerve, muscle
114024.e: A receptor picks up the stimulus and a sensory nerve carries it to the spinal cord. From there, a motor nerve carries the command to the muscle.
114024.m: A reflex arc runs from the sensory receptor through the spinal cord to the muscle.

114025.q: Why do reflexes happen especially quickly?
a: They are often switched in the spinal cord
They use the blood as a pathway
114025.e: With many reflexes, the signal does not have to go to the cerebrum first. The spinal cord switches straight to the muscle, which saves time.
114025.m: Reflexes are fast because the spinal cord reacts directly.

114026.q: Which inborn reflex makes newborn babies grip a finger tightly in their hand?
114026.e: If you touch the palm of a newborn baby, it closes its fingers firmly. This grasp reflex disappears in the first months of life.
114026.m: Newborn babies have a strong grasp reflex.

114027.q: What happens when you touch a hot hob?
a: You pull your hand away before you feel the pain
You feel pain first and then think
114027.e: The withdrawal reflex is triggered in the spinal cord. The pain signal takes longer to reach the cerebrum, so you feel the pain a little later.
114027.m: With heat, a reflex pulls your hand away even before you feel pain.

114029.q: What are the nerve pathways called that carry signals from the spinal cord to the muscles?
114029.e: Sensory nerves carry stimuli to the spinal cord. Motor nerves carry commands to the muscles.
114029.m: Motor nerves carry commands to the muscles.

114031.q: What does research say about the idea that there are “left-brained” and “right-brained” people?
a: It is a myth without evidence
114031.e: Studies found no evidence that some people mainly use one half of the brain. Both halves work together in almost all tasks.
114031.m: Everyone uses both halves of the brain.

114032.q: Which hand do about 90 per cent of people prefer?
a: A different one depending on the season
114032.e: About nine out of ten people are right-handed. Preferring one hand is an example of the halves of the brain being specialised in different ways.

114033.q: In which half of the brain are the most important language centres in the vast majority of right-handers?
114033.e: In the vast majority of right-handers, the left half of the brain is more important for language. This is a real specialisation, but not a personality type.
114033.m: In most people, language is mainly processed on the left.

114034.q: What connects the two halves of the brain?
114034.e: The corpus callosum is a thick bundle of nerve fibres. Through it, the two halves of the brain exchange information.
114034.m: The corpus callosum connects the two halves of the brain.

114035.q: Why was the corpus callosum between the halves of the brain cut in some people?
114035.e: In very severe epilepsy, cutting it could stop seizures from spreading to both halves. These patients are called split-brain patients.
114035.m: Split-brain operations were meant to ease severe epilepsy.

114036.q: What does lateralisation of the brain mean?
a: The halves of the brain specialise in some tasks
The brain lies at the side of the head
One half of the brain is always asleep
114036.e: Some tasks are processed more strongly in one half of the brain, for example language, usually on the left. Even so, both halves work closely together.
114036.m: Lateralisation means the halves of the brain have different focuses.

114037.q: Which statement about creativity and the halves of the brain is true?
a: Creative thinking uses both halves of the brain
Creativity is only in the right half
Creativity is only in the left half
Creativity is only in the cerebellum
114037.e: In creative thinking, networks in both halves of the brain work together. The idea of a purely “right-brain” creativity is greatly simplified.
114037.m: Creativity comes from both halves of the brain working together.

114038.q: Which half of the brain is more involved in recognising faces in most people?
114038.e: When recognising faces, the right half of the brain is more active in most people. Even so, both halves work together.
114038.m: We recognise faces mainly with the right half of the brain.

114039.q: Which animal's brain did the Blue Brain Project mainly want to recreate digitally?
114039.e: The goal was a detailed digital reconstruction of the mouse brain. Mice are often studied in brain research.
114039.m: The Blue Brain Project focused on the mouse brain.

114040.q: Who mainly funded the Blue Brain Project?
114040.e: The project was mainly funded with money from the Swiss Confederation. It was based at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne, the EPFL.
114040.m: The Swiss Confederation funded the Blue Brain Project.

114041.q: Which cells did the Blue Brain Project rebuild on the computer?
114041.e: The brain consists of billions of nerve cells. The project rebuilt them on the computer as accurately as possible to understand how the brain works.
114041.m: The Blue Brain Project simulated nerve cells.

114042.q: What was the goal of the Blue Brain Project?
a: To rebuild and simulate a brain digitally
To build a brain out of metal
114042.e: The project wanted to rebuild brain tissue on the computer, nerve cell by nerve cell, and simulate it.
114042.m: The Blue Brain Project wanted to recreate a brain on the computer.

114043.q: What did the Blue Brain Project need to simulate brain tissue?
114043.e: Simulating many nerve cells takes an incredible number of calculations. That is why the project ran on supercomputers.

114044.q: Why is it so difficult to simulate a whole human brain on a computer?
a: It has about 86 billion nerve cells
It has only ten nerve cells
It is made only of water
114044.e: Each nerve cell is connected to thousands of others. This huge number is beyond even today's supercomputers. That is why the Blue Brain Project first simulated small pieces of brain tissue.
114044.m: The human brain has about 86 billion nerve cells.

114045.q: At which university was the Blue Brain Project based?
114045.e: The project started in 2005 at the EPFL in Lausanne and ran until the end of 2024. Later it also worked in Geneva.
114045.m: The Blue Brain Project belonged to the EPFL in Lausanne.

114046.q: Which large EU brain research project started in 2013 with the EPFL taking part?
114046.e: The Human Brain Project was a flagship project of the EU and ran from 2013 to 2023. The EPFL coordinated it in the early years.
114046.m: The Human Brain Project was a large EU brain research project.

114047.q: Which sensory cells in the eye are responsible for seeing colour?
114047.e: The cones make colour vision possible in bright light. They are packed especially closely in the middle of the retina.
114047.m: We see colours with the cones.

114048.q: Why do we hardly see colours at dusk?
a: Then mainly the rods are working
114048.e: In low light, mainly the light-sensitive rods are working. They cannot tell colours apart, so everything looks grey.
114048.m: At dusk we see almost only shades of grey with the rods.

114049.q: How many types of cones does a person with normal vision have?
