114867.e: In 1905 Koch received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. It honoured his research on a serious infectious disease.
114867.m: Robert Koch received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1905.

114868.q: What did Robert Koch prove as one of the first people?
a: That blood circulates in the body
That the Earth goes round the Sun
114868.e: In 1876, using anthrax as an example, Koch showed that a particular bacterium causes a particular disease. That was a milestone in medicine.
114868.m: Koch proved that bacteria cause diseases.

114869.q: Which dangerous diarrhoeal disease often spreads through dirty drinking water?
114869.e: Cholera is spread by bacteria in dirty water. Robert Koch found the germ in India in 1884.
114869.m: Clean drinking water protects against cholera.

114870.q: What is the health institute in Berlin called that is named after Robert Koch?
114870.e: The Robert Koch Institute is Germany's central authority for infectious diseases. Koch was the institute's first director.
114870.m: The Robert Koch Institute in Berlin bears Koch's name.

114871.q: What did Robert Koch test with his famous rules?
a: Whether a germ causes a particular disease
114871.e: According to Koch's rules, a germ must be found in every sick person, be grown in a pure culture and cause the same disease in a healthy animal. They are called Koch's postulates.
114871.m: Koch's rules are used to test whether a germ causes a disease.

114872.q: Why was penicillin produced in large amounts during the Second World War?
a: To treat infected wounds of the injured
114872.e: In the past many wounded people died of wound infections caused by bacteria. With penicillin, these infections could be treated effectively for the first time.
114872.m: Penicillin saved many injured people in the Second World War.

114873.q: Where does penicillin originally come from?
114873.e: Penicillin is made by moulds of the genus Penicillium. They use it to kill bacteria around them.

114874.q: Which group of medicines does penicillin belong to?
114874.e: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them from growing. Penicillin was one of the first antibiotics.

114875.q: Which germs does penicillin work against, and which not?
114875.e: Penicillin attacks the cell wall of bacteria. Viruses do not have such a cell wall, so it does not help against flu, for example.
114875.m: Antibiotics help against bacteria but not against viruses.

114876.q: In which field did Alexander Fleming receive the Nobel Prize?
114876.e: Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with two researchers from Oxford. It honoured the discovery of penicillin and its use as a medicine.
114876.m: Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

114877.q: How did Fleming come to discover penicillin?
a: By chance, with a mouldy culture dish
Through a tip from a farmer
On an expedition to the jungle
114877.e: After his holiday, Fleming found a culture dish on which mould had grown. Around the mould the bacteria had died.
114877.m: Fleming discovered penicillin by a lucky accident.

114878.q: Why should you not take an antibiotic unnecessarily or incorrectly?
a: Because bacteria can otherwise become resistant
Because it otherwise turns into viruses
114878.e: If antibiotics are used wrongly or too often, tough bacteria survive and multiply. Then antibiotics no longer work.

114879.q: Which rays did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discover in 1895?
114879.e: Röntgen called the unknown rays “X-rays”. In German-speaking countries they are now called Röntgen rays after him.

114880.q: Which country did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen come from?
114880.e: Röntgen was a German physicist. He studied in Zurich and in 1895 discovered the rays named after him in Germany.

114881.q: What did the famous first X-ray image of a person show?
114881.e: At the end of 1895 Röntgen X-rayed the hand of his wife Anna Bertha. The picture shows the bones and her ring.
114881.m: The first famous X-ray image shows the hand of Röntgen's wife.

114882.q: Which famous award did Röntgen receive in 1901 as the very first physicist?
114882.e: The Nobel Prizes were awarded for the first time in 1901. Röntgen received the Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering X-rays.
114882.m: Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

114883.q: At which Swiss university did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen study?
114883.e: Röntgen studied mechanical engineering at the Zurich Polytechnic, today's ETH. Later he gained his doctorate at the University of Zurich.

114884.q: What can X-rays make especially easy to see?
114884.e: X-rays pass through soft tissue more easily than through bone. That is why bones appear light on the picture.
114884.m: Bones show up especially well on X-ray images.

114885.q: Why did Röntgen earn hardly any money from his discovery?
a: He sold it to the emperor
114885.e: Röntgen wanted his discovery to benefit everyone. That is why he did not take out a patent.
114885.m: Röntgen did not patent his discovery.

114886.q: Why do patients sometimes wear a lead apron when having an X-ray?
a: It protects parts of the body from the rays
114886.e: In large amounts, X-rays can damage cells. Lead blocks the rays well and so protects parts of the body that are not being examined.
114886.m: A lead apron protects against unnecessary rays during an X-ray.

114887.q: What is Florence Nightingale mainly known for?
a: As the founder of modern nursing
As the inventor of the clinical thermometer
114887.e: Florence Nightingale made nursing a respected profession with proper training. She placed great importance on cleanliness and fresh air.
114887.m: Florence Nightingale is seen as the founder of modern nursing.

114888.q: Besides nursing, in which field was Florence Nightingale also very gifted?
114888.e: Florence Nightingale collected figures and showed them in diagrams. In this way she showed how important cleanliness is in hospitals.
114888.m: Florence Nightingale used numbers to save lives.

114889.q: In which city was Florence Nightingale born, which also gave her her first name?
114889.e: She was born in Florence in 1820 while her parents were travelling. Her first name is the English form of the city's name.
114889.m: Florence Nightingale is named after her birthplace, Florence.

114890.q: Which international day is celebrated on 12 May, Florence Nightingale's birthday?
114890.e: Florence Nightingale was born on 12 May 1820. That is why nursing professions are honoured worldwide on this day.

114891.q: What did Florence Nightingale use to convince politicians of better hygiene?
114891.e: She collected figures on the causes of soldiers' deaths and drew clear diagrams from them. These showed that many died of avoidable diseases.
114891.m: Florence Nightingale convinced people with statistics and diagrams.

114892.q: What did most soldiers die of in the military hospital at Scutari before Nightingale's improvements?
114892.e: More soldiers died of diseases such as typhus and cholera than of their injuries. Dirt, bad water and cramped rooms helped the diseases spread.
114892.m: Most soldiers in the military hospital died of infections.

114893.q: Which Swiss city did Henry Dunant come from?
114893.e: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva on 8 May 1828. The Red Cross was later founded in Geneva as well.

114894.q: Which battle in Italy did Henry Dunant witness in 1859, after which he helped the wounded?
114894.e: At Solferino, thousands of wounded were left lying without help. Dunant organised their care with women from the village of Castiglione.
114894.m: Dunant witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859.

114895.q: Which aid organisation goes back to Henry Dunant?
114895.e: After what he saw on the battlefield of Solferino, Dunant worked for neutral help for the wounded. In 1863 the Red Cross was founded in Geneva.
114895.m: Henry Dunant is the founder of the Red Cross.

114896.q: Which international agreement to protect wounded soldiers was signed in Geneva in 1864?
114896.e: At the suggestion of the new committee in Geneva, twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention in 1864. It protects the wounded and medical staff in war.
114896.m: The first Geneva Convention of 1864 protects the wounded in war.

114897.q: Which prize did Henry Dunant receive in 1901 as one of the first winners?
114897.e: Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901 with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy. At that time he was living poor and withdrawn.
114897.m: Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

114898.q: Which day is celebrated on 8 May, Henry Dunant's birthday?
114898.e: On 8 May, Red Cross and Red Crescent societies around the world celebrate their founder. The day recalls the work of the helpers.
114898.m: 8 May is World Red Cross Day.

114899.q: Where are smallpox viruses still officially kept today?
a: In two high-security laboratories in the USA and Russia
In every hospital in the world
Nowhere in the world any more
114899.e: After smallpox ended, almost all virus samples were destroyed. Only two closely guarded laboratories in the USA and in Russia may still store samples.
114899.m: Smallpox viruses are officially stored in only two laboratories.

114900.q: Why was it possible to defeat smallpox completely?
a: The virus only infects humans, not animals
The virus dies out in winter
The virus only lives in water
114900.e: Because the smallpox virus only survives in humans, it could not hide anywhere. When everyone around a case was vaccinated, the chain of infection was broken.
114900.m: Smallpox could be defeated because the virus only infects humans.

114901.q: What kind of germ causes smallpox?
114901.e: Smallpox is caused by a very small disease particle that can only multiply in living cells. It is passed from person to person.
114901.m: Smallpox is caused by a virus.

114902.q: What did many people who had survived smallpox keep?
a: Scars on the face and skin
114902.e: Smallpox forms blisters filled with fluid on the skin. When they heal, they often leave deep scars.
114902.m: Smallpox often left scars on the skin.

114903.q: Where did the material for the first smallpox vaccination come from?
114903.e: The English doctor Edward Jenner used harmless cowpox for vaccination in 1796. The word vaccine comes from the Latin “vacca” for cow.
114903.m: The first smallpox vaccination came from cowpox.

114904.q: Why do people in Switzerland no longer need to be vaccinated against smallpox?
a: Because the disease has been wiped out
Because it can be cured with tea
Because smallpox only occurs in the tropics
114904.e: There have been no smallpox cases for decades, so the vaccination is no longer needed. General smallpox vaccination has therefore been stopped worldwide.
114904.m: People are no longer vaccinated against smallpox because it has been wiped out.

114905.e: The smallpox virus was passed on through coughing, talking or the blisters. That is why mainly people close to the sick were infected.
114905.m: Smallpox spread from person to person.

114906.q: By what name is the great wave of plague in Europe in the 14th century known?
114906.e: The pandemic in the 14th century is called the Black Death. It was one of the worst epidemics in history.
114906.m: The great plague of the 14th century is called the Black Death.

114907.q: Which animals spread the plague with their fleas?
114907.e: Fleas on rats carried the plague germ. When the fleas bit people, they infected them.

114908.q: How did the Black Death reach Europe?
a: On the wind from the desert
114908.e: Trading ships from the Black Sea brought the plague to Sicily. From there it spread across the whole of Europe.
114908.m: Trading ships brought the plague to Europe.

114909.q: Roughly what share of Europe's population died of the Black Death in the 14th century?
114909.e: Estimates suggest around 25 million deaths. That was about a third of Europe's population at the time.
114909.m: The Black Death killed about a third of the people in Europe.

114910.q: Where does the word “quarantine” come from?
a: From the Italian word for forty days
From the Latin word for illness
From the French word for harbour
From the Greek word for fear
114910.e: In Venice, ships from plague areas had to wait 40 days before anyone was allowed ashore. In Italian, forty is “quaranta”.

114911.q: What kind of germ causes the plague?
114911.e: The plague germ is a rod-shaped bacterium. Because it is a bacterium, plague can be treated with antibiotics today.
114911.m: The plague is caused by a bacterium.

114912.q: What did some plague doctors wear on their faces in the 17th century?
a: A mask with a long beak
114912.e: The beak was filled with sweet-smelling herbs. At that time people believed the plague was spread by bad air.
114912.m: Plague doctors wore masks with long beaks.

114913.q: Which form of plague occurs when the germ attacks the lungs and is passed on by coughing?
114913.e: In pneumonic plague, the bacteria get into the air when someone coughs. In this way it can be passed directly from person to person.
114913.m: Pneumonic plague is passed on by coughing.

114914.q: How can you recognise bubonic plague?
a: By green spots on the tongue
114914.e: In bubonic plague, the lymph nodes, for example in the armpit or neck, swell into painful lumps. That is where its name comes from.
114914.m: Bubonic plague shows itself through swollen lymph nodes.

114915.q: Which simple measure did Ignaz Semmelweis introduce in a Vienna hospital in 1847?
114915.e: Semmelweis demanded that doctors and students disinfect their hands before examinations. After that the number of deaths fell sharply.

114916.q: What happened after Semmelweis introduced hand disinfection?
114916.e: After it was introduced, the number of deaths in his ward fell sharply. That showed how important clean hands are.
114916.m: Thanks to hand disinfection, far fewer patients died.

114917.q: In which city was Ignaz Semmelweis working when he made his discovery?
114917.e: Semmelweis was an assistant doctor at the General Hospital in Vienna. There he compared the death rates of two wards.
114917.m: Semmelweis made his discovery in Vienna.

114918.q: In which century did Ignaz Semmelweis live?
114918.e: Semmelweis lived from 1818 to 1865. He made his discovery in Vienna in 1847.

114919.q: According to Semmelweis, where did the doctors bring the dangerous germs onto the ward from?
114919.e: Many doctors examined patients straight after dissecting dead bodies. Without washing their hands, they passed on deadly germs.
114919.m: The germs came from dead bodies on the doctors' hands.

114920.q: How did many doctors react to Semmelweis's demands at the time?
a: They made him the emperor's doctor
They gave him the Nobel Prize
114920.e: Many colleagues did not want to believe that their own hands spread diseases. Only after his death in 1865 were his ideas accepted.
114920.m: During his lifetime Semmelweis was rejected by many doctors.

114921.q: What did people not yet know at the time of Semmelweis, around 1847?
a: That water is needed for life
114921.e: It was only decades later that scientists proved bacteria cause diseases. So Semmelweis could not explain exactly why handwashing helped.
114921.m: Semmelweis worked before bacteria were known to cause disease.

114922.q: Why is Semmelweis seen today as a role model for hospital hygiene?
a: He showed that clean hands save lives
114922.e: His figures proved that the death rate fell sharply after hand disinfection was introduced. Hand hygiene is today the most important measure against hospital infections.
114922.m: Semmelweis showed that clean hands save lives.

114923.q: What is the flat glass dish for bacterial cultures called, invented by an assistant of Robert Koch?
114923.e: Julius Petri worked in Koch's laboratory in Berlin and developed the flat dish with a lid in 1887. It is still used in laboratories all over the world today.
114923.m: The Petri dish comes from Robert Koch's laboratory.

114924.q: In which city was Alexander Fleming working when he discovered penicillin?
114924.e: Fleming did research at St Mary's Hospital in London. Today there is a small museum in his former laboratory.

114925.q: What does a doctor promise in the medical oath, among other things?
a: To earn as much money as possible
114925.e: Since Hippocrates, doctors have promised to act for the good of the sick and not to harm them. Today there is a modern version, the Declaration of Geneva.
114925.m: Doctors promise not to harm the sick.

114926.q: In which test facility do cycling and ski teams measure the air resistance of their athletes?
114926.e: In a wind tunnel a large fan blows air past the person, who stays still. Sensors measure the braking force, so position and equipment can be improved.
114926.m: Air resistance is measured in a wind tunnel.

114927.q: Why do Formula 1 cars have big wings at the front and back?
a: They press the car onto the track
They make the car take off
114927.e: The wings are shaped the opposite way to an aeroplane's. They create downforce, so the car grips better and can go faster through corners.
114927.m: The wings of a racing car create downforce.

114928.q: Why are sprint and cycling records often easier to set in places high above sea level?
a: The thinner air slows you down less
There is no gravity there at all
114928.e: High up, the air density is lower. So air resistance falls, even though breathing is harder.
114928.m: In thin mountain air, air resistance is lower.

114929.q: What are the many small dimples on a golf ball for?
114929.e: The dimples create a thin, swirling layer of air around the ball. The air therefore separates later, the wake behind the ball gets smaller and the ball flies further.
114929.m: Dimples make a golf ball fly further.

114930.q: Why do cyclists in time trials wear helmets with a long, pointed shape?
a: So the air flows off better
114930.e: A streamlined shape lets the air flow smoothly back together behind the head. This creates fewer braking swirls.
114930.m: Streamlined helmets let the air flow off smoothly.

114931.q: What kind of bicycle wheel is often used at the back on the track to avoid air swirls from the spokes?
a: A wheel with twice as many spokes
114931.e: Spinning spokes churn up the air and slow you down. A closed disc wheel has no spokes and creates less resistance.
114931.m: Disc wheels reduce the air swirls from spokes.

114932.q: Which science studies how air flows around moving objects?
114932.e: The Greek word ‘aer’ means air. Aerodynamics studies air flows and the forces they put on objects.
114932.m: Aerodynamics studies how air flows around objects.

114933.q: Why are the racing suits of speed skaters and skiers very tight and smooth?
a: So the air slows them down less
So you can put them on faster
114933.e: Flapping fabric and folds create swirls and increase air resistance. Smooth, tight suits let the air flow past better.
114933.m: Tight, smooth suits reduce air resistance.

114934.q: Why is it forbidden in many triathlons to ride closely behind someone else on the bike course?
a: Because the slipstream gives an unfair advantage
Because the roads are too narrow
Because the bikes would have to crash
Because you would get too slow
114934.e: Anyone riding in the slipstream saves a lot of energy for the run that follows. That is why athletes in such races must keep a minimum distance.
114934.m: In many triathlons, riding in the slipstream is forbidden.

114935.q: In a group of cyclists, who has to work hardest against air resistance?
114935.e: The rider at the front meets the undisturbed air. The others ride in his slipstream.
114935.m: Air resistance is greatest at the front.

114936.q: Why do cyclists in a breakaway group take turns at the front?
a: So everyone can recover in the slipstream
So everyone is photographed equally often
So the bikes don't get hot
114936.e: Working at the front is tiring. By taking turns the effort is shared, and the group stays faster overall.
114936.m: Taking turns shares the work at the front.

114937.q: What do racing drivers use the slipstream of a car in front for?
114937.e: In the slipstream the resistance is lower, so the car behind gets faster. With this extra speed it then pulls out and passes.
114937.m: Racing drivers use the slipstream to overtake.

114938.q: What is a runner called who sets the pace at the front during record attempts and provides a slipstream?
114938.e: Pacemakers run a set distance at an even pace in front of the favourites. They can shelter from the wind behind them.

114939.q: Which runner, helped by many pacemakers, became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours, in Vienna in 2019?
114939.e: Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna in October 2019. Because the pacemakers changed during the run, the time does not count as an official world record.
114939.m: Kipchoge ran a marathon in under two hours in 2019.

114940.q: Why does the slipstream hardly matter for people walking slowly?
a: Because air resistance is very small at low speed
Because there is only a slipstream when it is windy
Because people don't create a slipstream
Because the air is warmer when walking
114940.e: Air resistance depends strongly on speed. Only at higher speeds, for example on a bike, is riding in the slipstream clearly worth it.
114940.m: The slipstream is worth it mainly at high speed.

114941.q: In which formation do large migrating birds often fly to save energy?
a: Stacked on top of each other
114941.e: Behind a bird's wingtips the air rises slightly. The birds behind use this updraught and save energy.
114941.m: Migrating birds save energy in a V formation.

114942.q: Apart from speed and the radius of the curve, what else does centrifugal force depend on?
114942.e: Centrifugal force is proportional to mass. An object twice as heavy is pushed outwards twice as strongly in the same curve.
114942.m: The greater the mass, the greater the centrifugal force.

114943.q: A car drives fast round a bend. Which way are the passengers pushed?
a: Towards the centre of the bend
114943.e: Because of its inertia, the body wants to keep going straight. But the car turns into the bend, so you feel pushed outwards. This effect is called centrifugal force.
114943.m: In a bend you feel the centrifugal force pushing outwards.

114944.q: Centrifugal force grows with the square of the speed. How does it change if you go round the same bend twice as fast?
a: It becomes four times as big
114944.e: You work out 2 squared, so 2 times 2. That gives 4. That is why going round bends too fast is so dangerous.
114944.m: Double the speed means four times the centrifugal force.

114945.q: At the same speed, how does the centrifugal force change when a bend gets tighter?
114945.e: Centrifugal force is inversely proportional to the radius of the bend. The tighter the bend, the more strongly you are pushed outwards.
114945.m: In tight bends the centrifugal force is greater.

114946.q: Which kitchen gadget uses centrifugal force to separate water from washed salad?
114946.e: In the fast-spinning spinner, the water flies outwards through the holes in the basket. The salad stays in the basket.
114946.m: The salad spinner separates water using centrifugal force.

114947.q: Why do the seats on a chair swing ride swing out at an angle?
a: Because of the centrifugal force as it turns
Because the chains are too long
114947.e: As it turns, centrifugal force pulls the seats outwards and gravity pulls them down. Together this gives a slanted position.
114947.m: On a chair swing ride, centrifugal force pushes the seats outwards.

114948.q: Why doesn't the water fall out when you swing a bucket quickly in a circle over your head?
a: Because the spinning presses it into the bucket
Because water sticks to the bucket
Because the air holds the water
114948.e: With enough speed, the effect of the spinning at the top is greater than gravity. The water is pressed against the bottom of the bucket.
114948.m: When spun fast, the water stays in the bucket.

114949.q: What is the lab device called that separates substances by their density by spinning very fast?
114949.e: In a centrifuge, heavier parts are pushed outwards more strongly than lighter ones. This is how, for example, blood cells are separated from blood plasma.
114949.m: A centrifuge separates substances by spinning fast.

114950.q: In which direction does the centripetal force point in circular motion?
a: Towards the centre of the circle
114950.e: The word comes from the Latin ‘centrum’ for centre and ‘petere’ for to seek. The force constantly pulls the object towards the centre.
114950.m: The centripetal force points towards the centre of the circle.

114951.q: In the hammer throw, what happens to the hammer as soon as the thrower lets go?
a: It flies off along a tangent
It keeps going round in a circle
114951.e: After letting go, the force that kept it on its circular path is gone. The hammer flies in the direction it was moving at that moment, that is, along a tangent.
114951.m: Without centripetal force, an object flies off along a tangent.

114952.q: In the hammer throw, what provides the centripetal force for the spinning hammer?
a: The steel wire the thrower pulls on
114952.e: The thrower holds the hammer by the wire and pulls it towards the centre. This keeps the ball on its circular path.
114952.m: In the hammer throw, the wire keeps the hammer on its circular path.

114953.q: What provides the centripetal force needed for a bicycle on a flat bend?
a: The friction between tyres and road
114953.e: The tyres press sideways against the road, and the grip acts towards the centre of the bend. On ice this friction is missing, which is why you slip.
114953.m: On a bend, tyre friction provides the centripetal force.

114954.q: Use F equals m times v squared divided by r: how big is the centripetal force on a cyclist and her bike of 60 kg at 10 m/s on a bend with a radius of 20 m?
114954.e: F is 60 kg times 10 m/s times 10 m/s divided by 20 m. That gives 6000 divided by 20, so 300 N.
114954.m: You calculate centripetal force as mass times speed squared divided by radius.

114955.q: Why are the bends of a cycling track steeply tilted inwards?
a: So that part of the centripetal force comes from the track
114955.e: On the sloping surface, the track also pushes the riders towards the centre of the bend. So they can ride fast without slipping sideways.
114955.m: Banked bends help provide the centripetal force.

114956.q: What is the inward tilt of a road or track bend towards its inside called?
114956.e: With banking, the outer edge is higher than the inner edge. This allows higher speeds through the bend.
114956.m: Banking raises the outer edge of a bend.

114957.q: Why do runners in the 200 m lean inwards on the bend?
a: So their feet create a force towards the centre of the bend
So they breathe in less air
So they can see the track better
114957.e: Because they lean, their feet push at an angle against the ground. The ground then pushes the runner towards the centre of the bend and keeps him on the track.
114957.m: Leaning into a bend creates the necessary force towards the centre.

114958.q: In which sport is the Fosbury Flop used?
114958.e: The Fosbury Flop is a technique for getting over the bar in the high jump. Today almost all high jumpers jump this way.
114958.m: The Fosbury Flop is a high-jump technique.

114959.q: Who is the Fosbury Flop named after?
114959.e: Dick Fosbury from the USA developed the technique in the 1960s. At first people laughed at him for it.
114959.m: The Fosbury Flop is named after Dick Fosbury.

114960.q: What happened after Dick Fosbury won Olympic gold with his new technique in 1968?
a: The technique spread around the world
114960.e: Fosbury's win convinced coaches and athletes. Within a few years almost all high jumpers were using the Flop.
114960.m: After Fosbury's Olympic win, the Flop spread quickly.

114961.q: How does a jumper cross the bar in the Fosbury Flop?
a: Face down with arms stretched out
114961.e: The jumper turns on take-off and goes over with his back to the bar. Head and shoulders go first, the legs last.
114961.m: In the Fosbury Flop you jump backwards, head first.

114962.q: Why has the Fosbury Flop almost completely replaced older high-jump techniques?
a: You can get higher over the bar with it
You don't need a run-up for it
It is the only technique allowed
114962.e: In the Flop, the body's centre of gravity can even stay below the bar while the body slides over it. So you can clear greater heights with the same strength.
114962.m: You jump higher with the Fosbury Flop.

114963.q: What was needed to make the Fosbury Flop possible without injuries?
a: Soft foam mats to land on
114963.e: In the past, high jumpers landed in sand or sawdust. Only with thick foam mats could you land safely on your back.
114963.m: Without soft mats the Fosbury Flop would be too dangerous.

114964.q: According to the rules, how must a high jumper take off?
a: From standing with a backwards run-up
114964.e: In the high jump only a one-footed take-off is allowed. In the Flop you take off from the foot further from the bar.
114964.m: In the high jump you take off from one foot.

114965.q: Roughly what is the men's high jump world record (as of 2026)?
114965.e: The Cuban Javier Sotomayor cleared 2.45 m in 1993. This record had not been beaten by 2026.
114965.m: The high jump world record is 2.45 m.

114966.q: What does the Magnus effect describe?
a: A spinning ball is pushed sideways
A ball bounces higher on hard ground
A ball gets lighter in water
114966.e: A ball that spins as it flies deflects the air flowing around it. This creates a sideways force, and the flight path curves.
114966.m: Because of the Magnus effect, a spinning ball flies in a curve.

114967.q: What must a flying ball do for the Magnus effect to happen?
a: It must stand still in the air
114967.e: Only a spinning ball deflects the air more on one side than on the other. This creates a sideways force. The effect is named after the physicist Heinrich Gustav Magnus.
114967.m: The Magnus effect only happens with spinning balls.

114968.q: In football, what do you call a ball that curves through the air because of its spin?
114968.e: The player strikes the ball on the side and gives it spin. Because of the Magnus effect, the ball then flies in a curved arc.
114968.m: A banana kick curves through the air because of spin.

114969.q: What does topspin, a forward spin, do to a tennis ball?
114969.e: Forward spin creates a downward force. The ball dips quickly behind the net and can still be hit hard.
114969.m: Topspin makes a tennis ball drop faster.

114970.q: What does backspin do to a golf ball that is hit a long way?
a: It gets lift and flies longer
It falls to the ground at once
114970.e: Through the Magnus effect, backspin creates an upward force. So the ball stays in the air longer.
114970.m: Backspin gives a golf ball lift.

114971.q: Which ship drive uses the Magnus effect with large spinning cylinders instead of sails?
114971.e: With a Flettner rotor, tall cylinders spin in the wind. This creates a sideways force that pulls the ship forwards.
114971.m: The Flettner rotor drives ships using the Magnus effect.

114972.q: How must a footballer strike the ball at a free kick so that it curves?
a: On the side, so it spins
Not at all, he must throw it
114972.e: If you strike the ball on the side, it gets spin. Because of the Magnus effect, it then flies in a curve.
114972.m: A ball struck on the side spins and curves.

114973.q: In the Magnus effect, what creates the force on the ball?
a: Different air flow on the two sides
114973.e: On one side the ball's surface moves with the air, on the other against it. The air is therefore deflected to one side, and the ball feels an opposite force.
114973.m: The Magnus effect comes from uneven air flow around the spinning ball.

114974.q: Why does a spin on the ice still slow down over time?
a: Because of friction from the blade and the air
114974.e: The blade and the air brake the spin a little. As a result, angular momentum is gradually lost.

114976.q: How can a figure skater slow down a spin without putting the other foot down?
114976.e: With arms spread out, the mass is further from the axis of rotation. The moment of inertia gets bigger and the spin slower.
114976.m: Spreading out your arms slows a spin.

114979.q: Which Swiss figure skater gave her name to a spin in which you pull your foot up over your head?
114979.e: Denise Biellmann became world champion in 1981. The Biellmann spin, named after her, is still performed today.
114979.m: The Biellmann spin is named after Denise Biellmann.

114980.q: Why does a diver spin faster in a tucked somersault than in a straight one?
a: Because his moment of inertia is smaller
114980.e: In the tuck, the mass is close to the axis of rotation. As with a skating spin, the smaller moment of inertia leads to faster spinning.
114980.m: You spin faster tucked than stretched out.

114981.q: In figure skating, what is the spin called in which you turn on one leg in a deep crouch?
114981.e: In the sit spin you bend the skating leg deeply and stretch the other leg forwards. The upright spin and the camel spin are the other basic forms.
114981.m: In the sit spin you turn in a deep crouch.

114982.q: At what launch angle does a ball fly furthest without air resistance, if it is thrown and lands at the same height?
114982.e: At 45 degrees, forward movement and flight time are split in the best way. Flatter throws land too early, steeper ones don't get far enough forward.
114982.m: Without air resistance, 45 degrees is the best launch angle.

114983.q: Do good long jumpers take off flatter or steeper than 45 degrees?
114983.e: To take off steeply, long jumpers would have to give up a lot of speed. That is why they take off much flatter, at about 20 degrees.
114983.m: Long jumpers take off flatter than 45 degrees.

114984.q: Why is the best release angle in the shot put a little smaller than 45 degrees?
a: Because the shot is released above the ground
Because the wind comes from the front
Because the shot is made of metal
114984.e: The shot starts at about shoulder height and lands on the ground. That gives it more flight time, and a flatter angle gives more distance.
114984.m: With a raised release point, a flatter angle is better.

114988.q: In which sport does the launch angle play a big role?
114988.e: In the javelin, besides speed, the angle also decides how far the javelin flies. A throw that is too steep or too flat costs distance.
114988.m: In throwing sports, the launch angle helps decide the distance.

114989.q: What happens with a vertical throw at a 90-degree angle without air resistance?
a: The ball lands back where it was thrown
The ball flies in a circle
The ball lands behind the thrower
114989.e: At 90 degrees the ball has no forward movement. It goes straight up and falls back down in the same place.
114989.m: A vertical throw has no throwing distance.

114990.q: Why do the pushers duck down low in the bobsleigh after getting in?
114990.e: If someone sticks out of the bob, the air brakes it more. Ducked down low, the bob has a smaller front surface.
114990.m: In a bob you duck down against air resistance.

114991.q: Why is the temperature of the runners checked before a bobsleigh race?
114991.e: Warmed runners reduce friction on the ice and make the bob faster. So that nobody cheats this way, the runners are compared with a reference.
114991.m: Runner temperature is checked because warm runners glide better.

114992.q: Why is the start so important in bobsleigh?
a: The push-off speed carries the bob down the whole track
Because you have to brake afterwards
Because only the start is timed
Because the bob then goes uphill
114992.e: Every tenth of a second the team gains when pushing affects the whole run. Later, the bob can hardly be speeded up any further.
114992.m: A fast start saves a lot of time in bobsleigh.

114993.q: What do bobsleigh riders feel particularly strongly in fast bends?
a: A big force pressing them into the seat
A force lifting them out of the bob
114993.e: In tight, fast bends, several times their body weight acts on the riders. They are pressed down hard into the bob.
114993.m: In bobsleigh bends the riders are pressed hard into the seat.

114994.q: Why is there a maximum weight for the bob and crew in bobsleigh?
a: Because heavier bobs would have an advantage
Because otherwise the track would melt
Because otherwise the start would be too easy
Because otherwise the runners would get too cold
114994.e: Going downhill, a heavy bob is slowed less by air resistance and friction than a light one. The maximum weight keeps conditions the same for all teams.
114994.m: The maximum weight ensures fair conditions in bobsleigh.

114995.q: Which energy is mainly turned into movement energy during a bobsleigh run?
114995.e: The bob starts at the top and travels many metres downhill. Its potential energy turns into movement energy, and part is lost as heat through friction.
114995.m: In a bob, height energy is turned into movement energy.

114996.q: Why does a bob have narrow, polished steel runners?
a: To keep friction on the ice low
114996.e: Smooth runners glide over the ice with little friction. So the bob loses less speed.
114996.m: Polished runners reduce friction on the ice.

114997.q: What is special about the bobsleigh run in St Moritz?
a: It is rebuilt from natural ice every winter
It is made entirely of wood
It is covered in plastic instead of ice
114997.e: The bob run from St Moritz to Celerina is made of natural ice. Every winter it is rebuilt by hand from snow and water.
114997.m: The St Moritz bob run is a natural ice track.

114998.q: Which ski position do ski jumpers use in flight today because it gives more lift?
114998.e: In the V shape, skis and body act like a wing. The air carries the jumper longer and he flies further.
114998.m: The V shape of the skis gives more lift in ski jumping.

114999.q: How did the judges first react when ski jumpers began jumping with their ski tips spread apart in the late 1980s?
114999.e: At first the new V style looked ugly to the judges, so points were deducted. But because you flew much further with it, everyone soon adopted this style.
114999.m: The V style was penalised at first and then caught on.

115000.q: Why is a light headwind good for ski jumpers?
115000.e: With a headwind, more air flows under the skis and body. This carries the jumper longer, which is why there is now a points adjustment for wind.
115000.m: A headwind gives more lift in ski jumping.

115001.q: Why are there strict rules on the size of ski jumping suits?
a: Loose suits would carry you like a sail
Loose suits would be too warm
Loose suits would be too heavy
Loose suits would be too expensive
115001.e: More fabric gives the air more surface and creates extra lift. The rules make sure the suits fit tightly.
115001.m: Suits that are too loose would act like sails.

115002.q: What is the number that gives the size of a ski jump, for example HS 140?
115002.e: The hill size is the distance in metres from the take-off table to the end of the landing area. It shows how far you can safely jump on a hill.
115002.m: The hill size gives the size of a ski jump.

115003.q: What does the K in the K-point of a ski jump stand for?
115003.e: The K-point is the point on the landing slope that the hill is designed around. On normal and large hills, anyone who jumps exactly to the K-point gets 60 distance points.
115003.m: The K in K-point stands for construction point.

115004.q: In which Swiss resort is a Ski Jumping World Cup held every year on the Gross-Titlis hill?
115004.e: The Gross-Titlis hill in Engelberg is the largest ski jump in Switzerland. The World Cup is usually held shortly before Christmas.
115004.m: Engelberg has the Gross-Titlis ski jump.

115005.q: Why do ski jumpers go down the in-run in a deep crouch?
a: To arrive at the take-off table faster
115005.e: In the crouch, air resistance is lower and the jumper reaches a higher speed. He can also push off powerfully from the crouch.
115005.m: A deep crouch on the in-run gives more speed.

115006.q: Which energy conversion is at the heart of the pole vault?
115006.e: The vaulter runs up fast and bends the pole. The pole straightens again and lifts the vaulter up, turning movement energy into height energy.
115006.m: In the pole vault, run-up energy is turned into height.

115007.q: What are modern vaulting poles usually made of?
115007.e: Fibre composites are light and bend a lot without breaking. In the past, people vaulted much lower with bamboo or metal poles.
115007.m: Modern poles are made of glass fibre or carbon fibre.

115008.q: Roughly how high do the world's best pole vaulters jump today?
115008.e: The best men today clear over 6 m, the best women about 5 m. That is higher than a two-storey house.
115008.m: Top vaulters clear over 6 m in the pole vault.

115009.q: Use h equals v squared divided by 2g: in theory, how high can the centre of gravity of a vaulter with a run-up speed of 10 m/s rise, if g equals 10 m/s²?
115009.e: h is 10 times 10 divided by 2 times 10, so 100 divided by 20. That gives 5 m, plus the height of the centre of gravity during the run-up.
115009.m: The faster the run-up, the higher a pole vaulter can go.

115010.q: Why is a fast run-up crucial in the pole vault?
a: More speed means more energy for height
So the vaulter needs to breathe less
115010.e: Movement energy grows with the square of the speed. The faster you run up, the more energy the pole can turn into height.
115010.m: A fast run-up provides the energy for great heights.

115011.q: What is the hollow in the ground called where the pole vaulter plants the pole on take-off?
115011.e: The bottom end of the pole rests in the planting box. Only then can the pole bend and lift the vaulter.
115011.m: On take-off, the pole is planted in the box.

115012.q: Which athlete has held the men's pole vault world record since 2020 and has improved it several times since (as of 2026)?
115012.e: Armand ‘Mondo’ Duplantis, who competes for Sweden, has kept raising the record by one centimetre at a time since 2020. In March 2026 he cleared 6.31 m in Uppsala.
115012.m: Armand Duplantis holds the pole vault world record.

115013.q: Why does a pole vaulter land on a thick mat after the bar?
a: To cushion the impact from a great height
So he can get up faster
115013.e: From over five metres up, the vaulter falls at high speed. The mat lengthens the braking distance and so reduces the force on the body.
115013.m: A thick mat cushions a fall from a great height.

115014.q: Why does a climbing rope for falls stretch on purpose?
a: So the fall is stopped more gently
115014.e: Because of the stretch, the climber is slowed over a longer distance. This reduces the force on the body and the anchor.
115014.m: A stretchy rope stops a fall more gently.

115015.q: What is a climbing rope called that stretches a lot in a fall?
115015.e: Dynamic ropes are made for falls and stretch noticeably. Static ropes hardly stretch and are used, for example, for abseiling.
115015.m: For belaying when climbing, you need a dynamic rope.

115016.q: How is a typical climbing rope built?
a: With a core and a protective sheath
From rubber with a fabric cover
115016.e: The core carries most of the load. The braided sheath protects the core from wear and dirt.
115016.m: A climbing rope has a core and a sheath.

115017.q: Why do you tie a knot in the end of the rope when climbing?
a: So the rope can't slip through the belay device
So you can see the rope better
115017.e: If the rope is too short, its end could slip through the belay device while lowering. The knot blocks it there and prevents a fall.
115017.m: A knot in the end of the rope stops it slipping through.

115018.q: The fall factor is the fall height divided by the length of rope paid out. A climber falls 4 m with 8 m of rope paid out. What is the fall factor?
115018.e: You work out 4 m divided by 8 m. That gives 0.5, so a fairly gentle fall.
115018.m: Lots of rope paid out makes a fall gentler.

115019.q: Why can a short fall close to the belay stance be especially hard?
a: Because there is little rope to absorb the fall
Because the rope is thicker there
115019.e: Close to the stance, only a little rope is paid out. The fall factor becomes large and the short rope has to absorb a lot of energy.
115019.m: Little rope between climber and belay makes falls hard.

115020.q: Why should a climbing rope not run over sharp rock edges?
a: The edge can damage the sheath and the core
It makes the rope too warm
115020.e: In a fall, the rope is dragged over the edge with great force. Sharp edges can fray it or even cut through it.
115020.m: Sharp edges are dangerous for climbing ropes.

115021.q: Why should a climbing rope be checked carefully or replaced after a very hard fall?
a: Because it may have lost some of its stretch
Because it is too heavy afterwards
115021.e: In hard falls the fibres are heavily strained. Afterwards the rope can absorb less energy and protects you less well.
115021.m: After hard falls a rope can absorb less energy.

115022.q: What is a belay device on the belayer's harness for when climbing?
a: It brakes the rope through friction
115022.e: The rope runs round tight bends in the belay device. The friction is so great that the belayer can hold a fall with little strength.
115022.m: A belay device brakes the rope with friction.

115023.q: In which unit is centripetal force given?
115023.e: Like every force, centripetal force is given in newtons. One newton accelerates a mass of 1 kg by 1 m/s².
115023.m: Forces such as centripetal force are measured in newtons.

115024.q: In tennis, what is a shot with backspin called in which the ball flies low and slowly?
115024.e: In a slice, the racket cuts down under the ball. The backspin keeps the ball in the air longer and makes it bounce low.

115025.q: In cycling, what do you call a line of team-mates who bring their sprinter to the front in their slipstream before the finish?
115025.e: The helpers ride at high speed in front of the sprinter and take turns. The sprinter saves energy in the slipstream for the last few metres.
115025.m: A lead-out train brings the sprinter to the front in the slipstream.

115026.q: With a simple identification key, how many options do you choose between at each step?
115026.e: At each step you choose between two features that rule each other out. Such a key is called dichotomous.
115026.m: A simple identification key gives two options each time.

115027.q: What do you get at the end if you have worked through a plant identification key correctly?
a: The name of the plant species
115027.e: An identification key leads step by step via features to a name. At the end there is usually the species or at least the genus.
115027.m: An identification key leads via features to the name of a plant.

115028.q: What do you find in the well-known identification book “Flora Helvetica”?
115028.e: The “Flora Helvetica” contains descriptions, photos and identification keys for the ferns and flowering plants of Switzerland. Flora means plant life.
115028.m: The Flora Helvetica is the well-known identification book for Swiss plants.

115029.q: How can you identify a plant when it is not flowering?
a: By its leaves, stem and growth form
Only by the scent of its flower
Only by the colour of its flower
115029.e: Even without flowers, leaf shape, leaf arrangement, stem and growth form reveal a lot about a plant. Special books such as the “Flora Vegetativa” use these features.
115029.m: Plants can also be identified by their leaves.

115030.q: In an identification key, what does the leaf arrangement “opposite” mean?
a: Two leaves sit facing each other at the node
The leaves only grow at ground level
Three or more leaves form a ring
115030.e: With opposite leaves, two leaves grow from a node on opposite sides. If there is only one leaf per node, this is called alternate.
115030.m: Opposite leaves sit in pairs facing each other.

115031.q: What does the feature “entire” mean for a leaf?
a: The leaf edge is smooth without teeth
The leaf has a red edge
The leaf has not been nibbled
115031.e: An entire leaf has a smooth edge without teeth, notches or cuts. The opposite is, for example, a serrated or toothed edge.
115031.m: An entire leaf has a smooth edge.

115032.q: What should you do if an identification key leads you to a plant that does not fit at all?
a: Go back and check a decision
Write down the name shown anyway
Pull the plant up and look for a new one
115032.e: A wrong result usually comes from answering a question about a feature wrongly. You go back step by step and check the decisions you were unsure about.
115032.m: If the result does not fit, go back through the key and check the steps.

115033.q: What do you call a leaf made up of several leaflets on the left and right of a central stalk?
115033.e: In a pinnate leaf, several separate leaflets sit on a shared stalk like a feather. Examples are the ash and the rowan.
115033.m: A pinnate leaf consists of many leaflets on one stalk.

115034.q: Which aid do you take outdoors to see small features such as tiny hairs when identifying plants?
115034.e: Many features such as glands, tiny hairs or minute flower parts are hard to see with the naked eye. A magnifying glass with about ten times magnification helps when identifying plants outdoors.
115034.m: With a magnifying glass you can see even tiny features when identifying plants.

115036.q: Which information must always be on the label of a herbarium specimen?
115036.e: Without the place and date, a specimen is almost worthless for research. The name of the plant and the name of the person who collected it are added too.
115036.m: Every herbarium label must show the place and date.

115037.q: What is the best way to dry plants for a herbarium?
a: In the sun on a plate
115037.e: The plant is laid flat between absorbent paper such as newspaper and weighed down. The paper is changed regularly so that the plant does not go mouldy.
115037.m: Herbarium plants are dried pressed between absorbent paper.

115038.q: Which plants must you not collect for your own herbarium?
115038.e: In Switzerland, protected species must not be picked or dug up. For a herbarium you choose common plants and take only a few specimens.
115038.m: Protected plants never belong in your own herbarium.

115039.q: What does a herbarium specimen from 1900 tell researchers today?
a: Where a plant used to grow
What the weather was like the next day
115039.e: The label shows the place and date it was found. This makes it possible to compare whether a plant still grows in the same place today or has disappeared.
115039.m: Old herbarium specimens show where plants used to grow.

115040.q: Which language does the word “herbarium” come from?
115040.e: “Herba” is the Latin word for herb or grass. So a herbarium is a collection of herbs and other plants.
115040.m: The word herbarium comes from the Latin herba, meaning herb.

115041.q: Why are old herbarium specimens often photographed and put on the internet today?
a: So that researchers worldwide can look at them
So that the plants can be thrown away
So that the plants turn green again
So that they can be sold in shops
115041.e: Digitising produces high-resolution images together with the label data. This lets experts all over the world compare specimens without travelling.
115041.m: Digitised herbarium specimens are available to researchers all over the world.

115042.q: What can still be obtained from old herbarium specimens today to study relationships between species?
115042.e: Remains of DNA survive even in dried plants. This allows relationships between species to be studied, even for plants that are rare today.
115042.m: DNA can still be obtained from old herbarium specimens.

115043.q: How do herbaria often protect their specimens from being eaten by insects?
a: They freeze the specimens for a while
They put the specimens in water
They put the specimens in the sun
They sprinkle the specimens with sugar
115043.e: Insects such as beetle larvae can eat dried plants. Freezing them for days at very low temperatures kills pests without damaging the specimen.
115043.m: Herbaria freeze specimens to kill pests.

115044.q: Why do researchers use scientific names for plants instead of common names?
a: They are clear and the same worldwide
115044.e: Common names differ from region to region and from language to language. A scientific name, on the other hand, refers to the same species everywhere in the world.
115044.m: Scientific names are clear all over the world.

115045.q: In which language are scientific plant names formed?
115045.e: Scientific names are Latin or are formed in a Latin way, even if they come from Greek or from people's names. Latin was the language of science for a long time.
115045.m: Scientific plant names are Latin or Latinised.

115046.q: How many words make up the scientific name of a species, for example Bellis perennis for the daisy?
115046.e: The first word names the genus, the second the species. This rule goes back to Carl Linnaeus.
115046.m: Scientific species names consist of two words.

115047.q: Which plants belong to the daisy family?
115047.e: In the daisy family, the “flower” is really a little basket of many tiny single flowers. Dandelions and ox-eye daisies also belong to it.
115047.m: The daisy and the sunflower belong to the daisy family.

115048.q: What does the species name “alba” mean in a scientific name such as Abies alba (silver fir)?
115048.e: “Albus” and “alba” mean white in Latin. For the silver fir this suits its pale grey bark.
115048.m: The Latin word alba means white.

115049.q: What does the species name “officinalis” mean, as in common sage (Salvia officinalis)?
115049.e: “Officina” was the workshop or pharmacy. Plants with the name “officinalis” were once used as medicinal plants.
115049.m: The name officinalis points to an old medicinal plant.

115050.q: What does the species name “sylvatica” mean for the common beech (Fagus sylvatica)?
115050.e: “Silva” means forest in Latin. The common beech is one of the most important forest trees in Switzerland.
115050.m: The name sylvatica means growing in the forest.

115051.q: Which rank in the classification of living things comes directly above the species?
115051.e: Several closely related species form a genus, several genera a family. So the order from the bottom is species, genus, family, order, class.
115051.m: In classification, the genus comes above the species.

115053.q: What is Carl Linnaeus especially famous for?
a: He built the first steam engine
115053.e: Linnaeus gave every plant and animal species a scientific name made of two words, for example Bellis perennis for the daisy. This system is still used today.
115053.m: Linnaeus gave species names made of two words.

115054.q: In which language are the scientific plant names after Linnaeus?
115054.e: Linnaeus wrote in Latin, the language of scholars in his time. That is why scientific names are still Latin today.

115055.q: Which part of the name “Bellis perennis” gives the genus of the daisy?
115055.e: The first word of a scientific name gives the genus, the second adds the species. This is how Linnaeus put nature in clear order.
115055.m: The first word in a scientific name is the genus.

115056.q: Why was Carl Linnaeus later called “Carl von Linné”?
a: He moved to the town of Linné
115056.e: Linnaeus was made a nobleman by the Swedish king in 1757. From 1761 he called himself Carl von Linné.
115056.m: Carl Linnaeus was ennobled and was then called Carl von Linné.

115057.q: Which abbreviation follows plant names given by Linnaeus, for example Bellis perennis?
115057.e: The scientific name is often followed by the name of the person who described the species. For Linnaeus, the letter “L.” is enough.
115057.m: The L. after a plant name stands for Linnaeus.

115058.q: Which subject did Carl Linnaeus study before he became famous as a botanist?
115058.e: Linnaeus studied medicine in Lund and Uppsala and qualified as a doctor in the Netherlands. Plants were important then because many medicines were made from them.

115059.q: How many parts does a species name have in binomial nomenclature?
115059.e: “Binomial” means having two names. The species name consists of the genus name and a species name, the epithet.
115059.m: A species name in binomial nomenclature has two parts.

115060.q: How do you write the two parts of a species name such as “Bellis perennis” correctly?
a: Genus with a capital, species name in lower case
Genus in lower case, species name with a capital
115060.e: The genus name always begins with a capital letter, the species name always with a small letter. This is true even when the species name comes from a person's name.
115060.m: The genus name has a capital letter, the species name does not.

115061.q: Why do we need scientific names such as Bellis perennis for the daisy?
a: So that everyone worldwide means the same species
So that the plant grows faster
So that the name sounds funnier
So that nobody understands the name
115061.e: Plants have different names in every language. The scientific name is the same everywhere, so researchers all over the world know which species is meant.
115061.m: Scientific names apply all over the world.

115062.q: The scientific name of the Swiss stone pine is Pinus cembra. Which part is the genus name?
115062.e: The first part, written with a capital letter, is the genus name. Pinus stands for the pines, to which the Swiss stone pine belongs.
115062.m: The first part of a species name is the genus.

115063.q: The genus name Urtica comes from the Latin “urere”, which means to burn. Which plant is meant?
115063.e: Urtica dioica is the common stinging nettle. Its stinging hairs break off when touched and release a burning liquid.
115063.m: Urtica dioica is the common stinging nettle.

115064.q: Which naturalist made two-part scientific species names well known?
115064.e: The Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus introduced the two-part names in the 18th century. We still use them today.
115064.m: Carl Linnaeus invented the two-part species names.

115065.q: How is a scientific species name usually written in printed texts?
115065.e: The genus and species name are set in italics so that they stand out from the rest of the text. By hand they are often underlined.
115065.m: Scientific species names are printed in italics.

115066.q: The scientific name of the red fox is Vulpes vulpes. What is striking about this name?
a: The genus and species name are the same
It is written all in lower case
115066.e: For animals, the genus name and species name may be the same, as with the red fox Vulpes vulpes. For plants this is not allowed.
115066.m: For animals, the genus and species name may be the same.

115067.q: In which language are scientific names such as Picea abies for the spruce mostly formed?
115067.e: Scientific names are formed from Latin or Greek. Picea abies is the spruce, the most common tree in Swiss forests.
115067.m: Scientific species names are mostly Latin.

115068.q: What do you do in a vegetation survey?
a: Note down all the plant species in an area
Dig up a tree and weigh it
115068.e: In a vegetation survey you choose a marked-out area and note down all the plant species in it. For each species you estimate how much of the area it covers.
115068.m: In a vegetation survey you note down all the plant species in an area.

115069.q: Which aid do you need in a vegetation survey to name unknown plants?
115069.e: With an identification book or an identification app, you can find out what a plant is called from its flowers and leaves. Only then can you note it down.
115069.m: Unknown plants are identified with an identification book.

115070.q: What do you estimate for each plant species in a vegetation survey?
115070.e: The cover shows what proportion of the area the plants of a species cover when seen from above. This shows which species are dominant.
115070.m: In a vegetation survey you estimate the cover of each species.

115071.q: A plant species covers 3 of the 4 square metres of a survey area. What is its cover?
115071.e: 3 out of 4 is three quarters. Three quarters is 75 per cent of the area.
115071.m: The cover shows what proportion of the area a species covers.

115072.q: What does it mean if a plant species has a very low cover?
a: It covers only a tiny part of the area
It covers almost the whole area
115072.e: The cover shows how much of the area a species covers when seen from above. A very low value means that only a few small plants of this species are present.
115072.m: A low cover shows a species that is rare in the area.

115073.q: Which layer is the lowest in a forest vegetation survey?
115073.e: In a forest, from top to bottom, you distinguish the tree, shrub, herb and moss layers. The cover is estimated separately for each layer.
115073.m: The moss layer is the lowest layer in the forest.

115074.q: Why must the area of a vegetation survey not be too small?
a: Otherwise many typical species are missing
Otherwise the plants do not grow
Otherwise it cannot rain on it
Otherwise the area is too hard to find
115074.e: On an area that is too small you only record some of the species. Only from a certain size are almost all the typical species present.
115074.m: A survey area must be big enough for all the typical species to be in it.

115075.q: Why do you mark out the area of a vegetation survey precisely, for example with string and pegs?
a: So that you only count species inside it
So that animals do not walk into it
So that the plants grow faster
So that the soil does not dry out
115075.e: Surveys can only be compared if there is a clear boundary. Species outside the area are not noted down.
115075.m: A marked-out area makes vegetation surveys comparable.

115076.q: Why are plant indicator values useful for experts?
a: You can judge the soil without measuring equipment
You can tell the time with them
You can tell the age of the plants
You can use them to sell plants
115076.e: If you know which plants grow where, you can work out from the plants present how moist, acidic or nutrient-rich the soil is.
115076.m: Indicator values help to judge the soil from the plants.

115077.q: What does a plant's indicator value show?
a: The conditions it usually grows in
How much it costs in a shop
115077.e: Indicator values show where a species is usually found, for example damp or dry, acidic or rich in lime. So you can work out what a site is like from its plants.
115077.m: An indicator value tells you the conditions a plant grows in.

115078.q: What does the moisture value (F) describe among the ecological indicator values?
115078.e: The moisture value shows how dry or wet the soil is where the plant typically grows. A low value means dry, a high value wet.
115078.m: The moisture value shows how damp the soil is.

115079.q: What does the reaction value (R) describe among the indicator values?
a: How acidic or rich in lime the soil is
115079.e: The reaction value describes the acidity of the soil. Low values show acidic soils, high values alkaline soils, often rich in lime.
115079.m: The reaction value shows how acidic the soil is.

115081.q: Four species grow in an area with moisture values of 2, 3, 4 and 3. What is the average moisture value?
115081.e: You add the values and divide by the number of species: (2 + 3 + 4 + 3) ÷ 4 = 12 ÷ 4 = 3. The average describes the area as moderately damp.
115081.m: The average indicator value is the mean of the values of all the species.

115082.q: What does the light value (L) describe among the indicator values?
115082.e: The light value shows whether a species tends to grow in the shade or in bright, open places. A low value means shady, a high value very bright.
115082.m: The light value shows how much light a plant needs.

115083.q: A plant has the highest moisture value. Where is it most likely to grow?
a: In a swamp or on a shore
115083.e: A high moisture value means that the plant needs wet soil. Such species grow in swamps, bogs and on shores.
115083.m: A high moisture value means a wet site.

a: Only professors are allowed to do research
Research only takes place in the laboratory
115084.e: In citizen science, interested people without specialist training collect data for research. Experts then analyse the data.
115084.m: In citizen science, non-experts help with research.

115085.q: What is the national data and information centre for the flora of Switzerland, to which you can report plant finds, called?
115085.e: Info Flora collects reports of finds from experts and non-experts. The data help to show how widespread and how endangered plants in Switzerland are.
115085.m: Plant finds in Switzerland are reported to Info Flora.

a: A short event where you find as many species as possible
A thunderstorm over a nature reserve
A quick method of drying plants
A race along a nature trail
115086.e: In a BioBlitz, experts and non-experts search an area together for a short time, often 24 hours, looking for as many animal and plant species as possible. This gives a snapshot of biodiversity.
115086.m: In a BioBlitz you look for as many species as possible in a short time.

115087.q: Which details make a plant record especially valuable for research?
a: Name and address of your parents
115087.e: With the place and date, a record can be put on a map and into a time series. A photo allows experts to check the identification.
115087.m: A good record includes the place, date and a photo.

115088.q: Why do experts check records from citizen science projects?
a: To punish the people who sent them
To count plants that do not exist
115088.e: Non-experts sometimes mix up similar species. Checking keeps the data reliable enough for research.
115088.m: Experts check citizen science data so that it stays reliable.

115089.q: In phenology, where non-experts can also help with research, what do you observe?
a: When plants come into leaf and flower
115089.e: Phenology records when in the year, for example, the hazel flowers or the beech gets its leaves. Records over many years show the effects of the climate.
115089.m: Phenology records when plants flower and come into leaf.

115090.q: Which photo is best if you want an identification app to recognise a plant?
a: Sharp close-ups of the flower and leaf
A blurred picture from far away
A photo of the whole meadow against the light
115090.e: Apps compare features such as flower shape and leaf edge with many reference pictures. The sharper and closer these features can be seen, the more reliable the result.
115090.m: Identification apps need sharp close-ups of the flower and leaf.

115091.q: What is the biggest advantage when many volunteers collect data for a research project?
a: You get data from a large area
The data are always free of mistakes
115091.e: Researchers on their own could never observe in so many places at the same time. Many volunteers provide data over large areas and many years.
115091.m: Thanks to many volunteers, research gets data from large areas.

115092.q: Which institution does the Botanical Garden in Bern belong to?
115092.e: The Botanical Garden of Bern is part of the University of Bern. It is used for teaching, research and by the public.
115092.m: The Botanical Garden of Bern belongs to the University of Bern.

115093.q: Which river is the Botanical Garden of Bern on?
115093.e: The garden lies on a sunny slope above the Aare in the Altenberg district. From there you look down on the river.
115093.m: The Botanical Garden of Bern lies on the slope above the Aare.

115095.q: Roughly how many plant species does the Botanical Garden of Bern show?
115095.e: According to the garden, around 5,500 different plant species from all over the world grow there. They include native species as well as tropical plants.
115095.m: Around 5,500 plant species grow in the Botanical Garden of Bern.

115096.q: How much does it cost to visit the Botanical Garden of Bern?
115096.e: The garden and the glasshouses can be visited free of charge. This makes it a popular place to relax in the middle of the city.
115096.m: The Botanical Garden of Bern can be visited for free.

115097.q: What does the Botanical Garden of Bern show in its alpine garden?
115097.e: An alpine garden is a rock garden with plants from the Alps and other mountains. This lets you see mountain plants without climbing a mountain.
115097.m: Plants from the mountains grow in the alpine garden.

115098.q: Which glasshouse is there in the Botanical Garden of Bern?
115098.e: Palms, ferns and succulents, among others, grow in the glasshouses. It is warm there even in winter.
115098.m: You can visit a palm house in the Botanical Garden of Bern.

115099.q: Apart from showing plants, what job does a university garden such as the Botanical Garden of Bern have?
115099.e: Botanical gardens collect plants for teaching and research. They also help to preserve rare and endangered species.
115099.m: Botanical gardens are used for research and for preserving rare plants.

115100.q: Roughly how old is the botanical garden in Geneva?
115100.e: The botanical garden in Geneva was founded in 1817. In 2017 it celebrated its 200th anniversary.
115100.m: The botanical garden in Geneva is over 200 years old.

115101.q: Which language is mainly spoken in Geneva, where the Jardin botanique is?
115101.e: Geneva lies in western Switzerland, where French is spoken. That is why the garden is called “Jardin botanique”.
115101.m: Geneva is in the French-speaking part of Switzerland.

115102.q: Which lake is the botanical garden in Geneva on?
115102.e: The garden lies on the right bank of Lake Geneva, not far from the Palais des Nations.
115102.m: The botanical garden in Geneva is on Lake Geneva.

115103.q: What is a herbarium, like the one the botanical garden in Geneva has?
a: A collection of pressed, dried plants
115103.e: In a herbarium, plants are pressed, dried, labelled and stored. The Geneva herbarium, with over six million specimens, is one of the largest in the world.
115103.m: A herbarium is a collection of dried plants.

115104.q: Roughly how big is the botanical garden in Geneva?
115104.e: The garden covers around 28 hectares. That is about the size of 40 football pitches.
115104.m: The botanical garden in Geneva covers around 28 hectares.

115105.q: Why did the botanical garden in Geneva move from the old town to the lake in 1904?
a: The plants wanted a lake view
The old garden became a railway station
115105.e: At first the garden was in the old town in the Parc des Bastions. In 1904 it moved to its present, much larger site on Lake Geneva.
115105.m: The botanical garden in Geneva moved to the lake because it needed more space.

115106.q: Who owns the Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de Genève?
115106.e: The full name is “Conservatoire et Jardin botaniques de la Ville de Genève”. So it is an institution of the City of Geneva.
115106.m: The botanical garden in Geneva is an institution of the City of Geneva.

115107.q: What does “Conservatoire” mean in the name of the Geneva institution?
a: The part with the herbarium and research
115107.e: In the Conservatoire, plants are preserved and studied, mainly in the herbarium and the library. The Jardin is the public garden.
115107.m: In the Geneva Conservatoire, plant collections are preserved and studied.

115108.q: What is a field notebook in nature research?
115108.e: In a field notebook you record observations directly out in the field. That way no information is lost before you get home.
115108.m: In a field notebook you note down observations right there outdoors.

115109.q: What is the best thing to write with in a field notebook so that nothing smudges when it rains?
115109.e: Pencil does not run when it gets wet and stays readable for a long time. Ink can smudge in the rain.
115109.m: In a field notebook you write in pencil, because it does not run in the rain.

115110.q: What do you note down first for each observation in a field notebook?
115110.e: Without the date and place, you cannot make sense of an observation later. Then come details such as species, number and habitat.
115110.m: Every field observation needs a date and place.

115111.q: How can you give a place of finding especially precisely in a field notebook?
a: With the name of the weather
With the colour of the sky
115111.e: Coordinates, for example from a mobile phone or a national map, describe a place very precisely. This means you can find the spot again later.
115111.m: Coordinates let you give a place of finding precisely.

115112.q: Why do people often draw small sketches in a field notebook?
a: Drawing is compulsory in the forest
115112.e: When you draw, you look more closely and record the shapes of leaves or flowers. A sketch can also show what remains unclear in a photo.
115112.m: Sketches in a field notebook help to record features precisely.

115113.q: When should you write observations in your field notebook?
a: At the end of the holidays
115113.e: Memories quickly become inaccurate. If you write things down straight away, you reliably record details such as number, time or location.
115113.m: You write observations in the field notebook straight away, on the spot.

115114.q: What is a collection number in a field notebook for, when you also collect plants for a herbarium?
a: It links the note and the specimen
It shows the price of the plant
It counts the steps you have walked
It gives the number of flowers
115114.e: Each plant collected gets a number that is also written in the field notebook. This way you know later which notes belong to which specimen.
115114.m: A collection number links the herbarium specimen with the notes in the field notebook.

115115.q: On which ship did Charles Darwin keep many field notebooks on his voyage around the world?
115115.e: Darwin sailed around the world on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836. His notebooks later formed the basis for many discoveries.
115115.m: Charles Darwin filled many field notebooks on the Beagle.

115116.q: Why do you see a three-dimensional image through a stereo microscope?
a: Each eye has its own light path
It always magnifies a thousand times
115116.e: A stereo microscope has a separate light path for each eye with a slightly different angle of view. The brain puts the two images together into a three-dimensional impression.
115116.m: Thanks to two light paths, the stereo microscope shows a three-dimensional image.

115117.q: Which lighting do you usually use with a stereo microscope to look at a whole flower?
115117.e: Objects that light cannot pass through, such as flowers, seeds or insects, are lit from above. The light is reflected from the surface.
115117.m: With a stereo microscope, objects are usually lit from above.

115118.q: What do you usually not need with a stereo microscope, unlike an ordinary light microscope?
115118.e: With a stereo microscope you look at whole objects. With a microscope where light shines through, on the other hand, specimens must be thin enough for light to pass through.
115118.m: With a stereo microscope you can look at whole objects without thin slices.

115119.q: What else is a stereo microscope often called in Swiss schools?
115119.e: Because you look into it with both eyes at the same time, it is often called a binocular. “Bini” is Latin and means two at a time.
115119.m: A stereo microscope is often called a binocular, because you look with both eyes.

115120.q: How strongly does a stereo microscope magnify compared with a light microscope for cells?
115120.e: A stereo microscope usually only magnifies up to about a hundred times, often much less. To see single cells you need a light microscope with stronger magnification.
115120.m: A stereo microscope magnifies less than a light microscope for cells.

115121.q: Why is it easy to work with tweezers and a needle under a stereo microscope?
a: It has a large working distance
115121.e: There is plenty of space between the lens and the object. That is why you can, for example, take a flower apart under the microscope.
115121.m: The large working distance allows dissecting under the stereo microscope.

115122.q: How does the image in a stereo microscope appear compared with the object?
a: Upright and the right way round
115122.e: Prisms in the stereo microscope turn the image so that it appears upright and the right way round. If you move the object to the left, it also moves to the left in the image.
115122.m: In a stereo microscope the image is upright and the right way round.

115123.q: Which of these objects is best examined with a stereo microscope?
115123.e: Whole small objects such as flowers, seeds or tiny moss plants are ideal. Bacteria, viruses and atoms are far too small for it.
115123.m: With a stereo microscope you examine whole small objects.

115124.q: Which invention comes from the Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral?
115124.e: Georges de Mestral developed a fastener made of two strips that stick to each other. Today you find it on shoes, jackets and bags.

115125.q: At which event in 1969 was Velcro present?
a: The opening of the Gotthard road tunnel
115125.e: Velcro helped the astronauts hold objects in place in weightlessness. So the Swiss invention was on the moon in 1969.
115125.m: Velcro flew on the first moon landing in 1969.

115126.q: During which pastime did Georges de Mestral make the observation that led to his invention?
115126.e: De Mestral came home from a hunt with his dog. Lots of burrs were stuck in the dog's fur.
115126.m: Georges de Mestral made his discovery after a hunt with his dog.

115127.q: What did Georges de Mestral discover when he looked at a burr under the microscope?
115127.e: The burdock's seed heads have lots of fine hooks. These get caught in fibres and hair without breaking off.
115127.m: Burrs stick thanks to tiny elastic hooks.

115128.q: What are the two sides of a Velcro fastener made of?
115128.e: One side has lots of little hooks, the other lots of soft loops. If you press them together, they hook into each other.
115128.m: Velcro has hooks on one side and loops on the other.

115129.q: Why did Georges de Mestral apply for a patent for his Velcro fastener?
a: So that nobody could simply copy the invention
So that he could give it away
So that it would be shown in a museum
So that he no longer had to make it
115129.e: A patent protects an invention for a certain time. De Mestral registered Velcro in Switzerland in 1951.
115129.m: A patent protects an invention from copycats.

115130.q: From which two French words was the brand name “Velcro” formed?
115130.e: “Velours” is a velvety fabric that is like the loop side. “Crochet” means hook and stands for the hook side.
115130.m: The name Velcro combines the words velours and crochet.

115131.q: What is it called when technology copies models from nature, as with Velcro?
115131.e: Bionics transfers solutions from nature to technology. Velcro is seen as one of the best-known examples.
115131.m: When technology copies nature, it is called bionics.

115132.q: Which canton did Georges de Mestral come from?
115132.e: Georges de Mestral was born in 1907 in Saint-Saphorin-sur-Morges in the canton of Vaud. He studied at the technical university in Lausanne.
115132.m: Georges de Mestral was an engineer from the canton of Vaud.

115133.q: Which transparent material did the Swiss chemist Jacques Edwin Brandenberger invent?
