115534.e: Phosphates got into the water with the waste water and made algae grow strongly. When the algae broke down, oxygen was removed from the lakes.
115534.m: Phosphate in waste water makes algae spread in lakes.

115535.q: Which ingredient in washing powder removes coloured stains such as tea or red wine?
115535.e: Bleaches such as sodium percarbonate release oxygen during washing. This destroys the dyes in the stains.
115535.m: Bleach destroys the dyes in stains.

115536.q: Why does washing at 30 instead of 60 degrees Celsius save energy?
115536.e: Most of a washing machine's energy is used to heat the water. Modern washing powders with enzymes work well even at low temperatures.

115537.q: What is making soap from fat and lye called?
115537.e: If you boil fats or oils with a lye, they split into glycerol and soap. This process is called saponification.
115537.m: Soap is made from fat and lye.

115538.q: Which part of a soap particle holds on to the grease?
115538.e: Soap particles have a long hydrocarbon tail that dissolves in fat and a charged head that points into the water.
115538.m: Soap particles are half fat-loving and half water-loving.

115539.q: How does soap remove grease from your hands?
a: Soap particles surround the grease and water rinses it away
Soap makes the grease rock hard
115539.e: Many soap particles gather around a droplet of grease and form a tiny ball, a micelle. This floats in the water and is rinsed away.
115539.m: Soap wraps up grease so water can rinse it away.

115540.q: Why is washing your hands with soap good against flu or coronaviruses?
115540.e: Many viruses such as flu and coronaviruses have an envelope made of fatty substances. Soap dissolves this envelope, and the viruses are rinsed off together with the dirt.
115540.m: Soap dissolves the fatty envelope of many viruses.

115541.q: What forms when soap dissolves in very hard water?
115541.e: Calcium and magnesium ions form insoluble lime soap with soap. It shows up as a grey ring in sinks and bathtubs.
115541.m: In hard water, soap forms lime soap.

115542.q: Why does a paper clip floating on water sink when you add soap to the water?
115542.e: Surface tension acts like a thin skin that carries the light paper clip. Soap weakens this skin, and the clip sinks.
115542.m: Soap weakens the surface tension of water.

115543.q: How does a solution of plain hard soap and water react?
115543.e: Soap is the salt of a weak fatty acid and a strong lye. Its solution therefore has a pH value well above 7.

115544.q: Which soap is soft and often used for cleaning floors?
115544.e: Soft soap is made with potassium hydroxide and stays soft. Solid soaps such as hard soap are made with sodium hydroxide.
115544.m: Soft soap is soft, hard soap is solid.

115545.q: Without protection, your skin goes red after 10 minutes. In theory, how long at most does a cream with sun protection factor 20 protect you?
115545.e: The sun protection factor is multiplied by your own protection time: 10 minutes times 20 gives 200 minutes. Experts advise using only about 60 per cent of that.
115545.m: Sun protection factor times your own protection time gives the theoretical protection time.

115546.q: Which UV radiation mainly causes sunburn?
115546.e: UV-B is high in energy and damages the top layer of skin, which leads to redness. The sun protection factor mainly refers to this range.

115547.q: What does UV-A radiation mainly do in the skin?
a: It goes deep and makes the skin age
It warms the skin without any effect
It makes the skin wet at once
115547.e: UV-A reaches deeper layers of skin and damages the elastic fibres there. This encourages wrinkles and can also contribute to skin cancer.
115547.m: UV-A makes the skin age early.

115548.q: Which substances do mineral sunscreens use as filters?
115548.e: Tiny particles of titanium dioxide and zinc oxide absorb most of the UV radiation. Only a small part is scattered or reflected.
115548.m: Mineral filters consist of tiny particles of metal oxides.

115549.q: What does putting cream on again after swimming do?
a: It keeps up the protection but does not extend it
It makes the skin brown at once
It is never needed with sun cream
115549.e: Water and drying off remove some of the cream. Putting more on restores the protection, but the maximum protection time does not start again.
115549.m: Putting on more cream does not extend the protection time.

115550.q: From which UV index is sun protection recommended?
115550.e: According to the World Health Organization, a UV index of 3 or more means a moderate level at which you should protect yourself.
115550.m: From UV index 3, you need sun protection.

115551.q: How does UV radiation change as you climb higher in the Swiss Alps?
115551.e: At altitude, the layer of air above you is thinner and filters out less UV radiation. That is why you need especially good sun protection in the mountains.
115551.m: UV radiation is stronger in the mountains.

115552.q: Why is sun protection especially important when skiing?
a: Snow produces its own UV radiation
The sun shines longer in winter
115552.e: Fresh snow reflects a large part of the UV radiation. The skin is then hit from above and below.

115553.q: What is the main aim of preserving food?
a: To slow down the growth of microorganisms
To make the taste ever sweeter
115553.e: Bacteria, yeasts and moulds make food go off. Preserving methods take away their water, warmth or oxygen, or kill them.

115554.q: Why does salted fish keep for a long time?
a: The salt draws water out of bacteria
The salt makes the fish cold
The salt forms a plastic layer
115554.e: Through osmosis, salt draws water out of the food and out of the bacterial cells. Without enough free water, germs can hardly multiply.

115555.q: Why do gherkins pickled in vinegar keep for a long time?
115555.e: Vinegar lowers the pH value a lot. In such an acidic environment, most bacteria that cause rotting cannot multiply.
115555.m: Acidic food goes off more slowly.

115556.q: Who is considered the inventor of preserving food by heating it in airtight containers?
115556.e: At the beginning of the 19th century, the French cook Nicolas Appert heated food in sealed glass bottles. He is seen as the founder of tinned and bottled food.

115557.q: Why does jam go off only slowly despite the fruit?
a: Lots of sugar binds the water
The jar is coated with salt inside
115557.e: The high sugar content binds the water, so microorganisms find hardly any free water. In addition, the jam is filled into jars while hot.

115558.q: Why does dried fruit hardly go off?
a: It contains only a little water
It contains a lot of salt
115558.e: When drying, most of the water is removed from the fruit. Without water, bacteria and moulds can hardly multiply.
115558.m: Dried food keeps for a long time.

115559.q: What does cooling in the fridge do to most bacteria?
115559.e: Cold slows down the bacteria's metabolism, but does not kill most of them. That is why even chilled food goes off after a while.
115559.m: Cooling slows bacteria down but usually does not kill them.

115560.q: Why does vacuum-packed meat keep longer?
a: Many germs need oxygen to grow
It is very hot in a vacuum
The vacuum makes the meat dry
115560.e: When vacuum packing, the air is sucked out of the packaging. Without oxygen, many spoilage germs grow more slowly, and the fat goes rancid less quickly.
115560.m: Without oxygen, food goes off more slowly.

115561.q: Which old preserving method uses the smoke of smouldering wood?
115561.e: When smoking, the surface of the food dries, and substances from the smoke slow down microorganisms. This makes ham or fish, for example, keep longer.
115561.m: Smoking makes meat and fish keep longer.

115562.q: What is the difference between sterilising and pasteurising?
115562.e: Sterilising heats well above 100 degrees Celsius. This kills all germs, including tough spores, which pasteurising does not.
115562.m: Sterilising kills all germs, pasteurising only most.

a: Brief heating below 100 degrees kills most germs
Exposure to light colours the milk
115563.e: A food is briefly heated to a temperature below boiling point. This kills most germs that cause illness.

115564.q: Roughly which temperature is milk heated to in short-time pasteurisation?
115564.e: In short-time heating, milk is heated to about 72 to 75 degrees Celsius for about 15 to 30 seconds and then cooled immediately.
115564.m: Pasteurised milk was only heated briefly.

115565.q: Why does unopened UHT milk keep for months without refrigeration?
a: It was briefly heated to a very high temperature
It contains a lot of salt
115565.e: UHT means ultra-high temperature: the milk is heated to over 135 degrees Celsius for a few seconds. This kills almost all germs, including most spores.
115565.m: UHT milk keeps for a long time.

115566.q: Among other things, pasteurising protects against which once-feared illness from cow's milk?
115566.e: In the past, germs of bovine tuberculosis could be passed on to humans through raw cow's milk. Pasteurising reliably kills these bacteria.
115566.m: Pasteurising protects against germs in milk.

115567.q: For which drink did Louis Pasteur originally develop the process?
115567.e: In the 1860s Pasteur investigated why wine goes off. He showed that brief warming kills the harmful microorganisms.
115567.m: Wine was the first thing to be pasteurised.

115568.q: From which milk is the Swiss cheese Le Gruyère AOP made?
115568.e: Unheated raw milk is used for Le Gruyère AOP. The long ripening and the way it is made ensure safety and the typical taste.
115568.m: Many Swiss hard cheeses are made from raw milk.

115569.q: What advantage does pasteurisation have over long boiling?
a: Taste and vitamins are better preserved
It is guaranteed to kill all spores
It makes food keep for years
It needs no energy at all
115569.e: Because the food is heated less strongly and for less time than when boiling, the taste, appearance and heat-sensitive vitamins change less.

a: Frozen water evaporates in a vacuum
The food is dried in the sun
115570.e: The food is frozen first. Then the air pressure in a chamber is lowered a lot, and the ice turns directly into water vapour.
115570.m: In freeze-drying, ice disappears directly as vapour.

115571.q: What is the direct change from solid to gas called?
115571.e: In sublimation, a solid becomes a gas without first becoming liquid. This happens to the ice in freeze-drying.
115571.m: Sublimation goes directly from solid to gas.

115572.q: Why is a vacuum needed for freeze-drying?
a: Ice only sublimates quickly at very low pressure
It gets very hot in a vacuum
The vacuum kills bacteria at once
115572.e: At normal air pressure, the ice would first melt when warmed. At very low pressure, however, it turns directly into vapour.
115572.m: Without low pressure, the ice would first turn liquid.

115573.q: Which well-known drink powder is often freeze-dried?
115573.e: For instant coffee, strong coffee is frozen and freeze-dried. With hot water, it quickly becomes a drink again.
115573.m: Instant coffee is often freeze-dried coffee.

115574.q: Why do mountaineers like taking freeze-dried meals with them?
115574.e: Because almost all the water has been removed, the meals weigh very little. On the way, you add hot water.
115574.m: Freeze-dried food is light to carry.

115575.q: What advantage does freeze-drying have over drying with heat?
a: Shape, flavour and nutrients are better preserved
115575.e: Because the food stays cold, heat-sensitive flavours and vitamins are protected. The shape also stays largely the same.

115576.q: Why does freeze-dried food keep for a long time?
a: Without water, germs can hardly multiply
It contains a lot of sugar
115576.e: Bacteria and moulds need water to grow. Because almost all the water has been removed, the food hardly goes off.
115576.m: Without water, food goes off much more slowly.

115577.q: Why do freeze-dried strawberries soak up water again very quickly?
a: They are full of tiny pores
They contain a lot of salt
115577.e: Where there were ice crystals before, fine holes are left after drying. Water quickly gets back in through this porous structure.
115577.m: Freeze-dried food is porous like a sponge.

115578.q: What does the non-stick coating of a frying pan do?
a: The pan stays cool on the outside
115578.e: Many non-stick pans are coated with the plastic PTFE. Water, fat and bits of food hardly stick to it.
115578.m: Food hardly sticks to a non-stick coating.

115579.q: How was the non-stick plastic PTFE discovered in 1938?
a: Through a find in a cave
115579.e: A chemist was investigating refrigerants and found a white, waxy powder in a gas cylinder. It was PTFE, which later turned out to be very slippery and heat-resistant.

115580.q: How can you tell that a non-stick pan should be replaced?
a: The coating is scratched or peeling off
The handle gets warm when cooking
115580.e: If the coating is damaged, food sticks and small particles can come loose. Then it is time for a new pan.
115580.m: A scratched non-stick pan should be replaced.

115581.q: Why does hardly anything stick to a PTFE coating?
a: Other substances are hardly attracted to it
115581.e: The fluorine atoms on the surface form almost no attractive forces with other substances. That is why water and fat roll off and food comes away easily.
115581.m: Non-stick surfaces hardly attract other substances.

115582.q: Why shouldn't you stir with a metal fork in a coated pan?
115582.e: Metal edges can scratch the thin coating. Food sticks to damaged spots, and the layer peels off over time.
115582.m: Use wooden or plastic utensils with coated pans.

115583.q: Why shouldn't you heat an empty coated pan on the highest setting?
a: The coating can break down and give off fumes
The hob switches off for ever
115583.e: An empty pan gets very hot very quickly. At too high temperatures, PTFE can break down and give off harmful fumes.
115583.m: Never overheat an empty non-stick pan.

115584.q: Which other kind of non-stick coating is made without PTFE?
115584.e: Ceramic coatings consist of a glass-like layer based on silicon. They are also non-stick, but often wear out faster.
115584.m: Ceramic is an alternative to PTFE.

115585.q: What else do plumbers use PTFE for?
115585.e: Thin PTFE tape is wrapped around threads. It seals the joint and makes screwing it together easier.

115586.q: What do the E numbers on food packaging refer to?
115586.e: Every food additive approved in the EU and Switzerland has an E number. This means it can be recognised whatever the language.

115587.q: Why is vitamin C added to apple juice, for example?
a: So that it does not turn brown
115587.e: Vitamin C, E 300 on packaging, protects against oxygen. This keeps the colour of the juice fresh for longer.
115587.m: Vitamin C stops food changing colour.

115588.q: What is citric acid often used for in drinks and sweets?
115588.e: Citric acid, E 330 on packaging, is an acidifier. It occurs naturally in lemons.

115589.q: What is an emulsifier such as lecithin in chocolate or margarine for?
115589.e: Fat and water normally do not mix. Emulsifiers have a fat-loving and a water-loving part and so keep both evenly spread.

115590.q: What is the gelling agent agar-agar obtained from?
115590.e: Agar-agar is obtained from the cell walls of certain red algae. It is a plant-based alternative to gelatine.
115590.m: Agar-agar is a gelling agent made from algae.

115591.q: Which gelling agent from apples or citrus peel is used for jam?
115591.e: Pectin is part of plant cell walls. Together with sugar and acid, it makes jam set.

115592.q: What are antioxidants used for in food?
a: So that fats do not go rancid
115592.e: Oxygen from the air can change fats and colourings. Antioxidants slow this reaction down, so food stays fresh longer.

115593.q: What do preservatives such as sorbic acid do?
a: They slow down moulds and yeasts
They make dough light and airy
115593.e: Sorbic acid (E 200) slows the growth of moulds and yeasts. It is used, for example, in baked goods or cheese.

115594.q: Which country runs the satellite navigation system GPS?
115594.e: GPS was built by the US Department of Defense and is now freely available to civilian users worldwide.
115594.m: GPS is the navigation system of the USA.

115596.q: Where are the satellites of a navigation system such as GPS?
a: At a height of 10 km like aeroplanes
115596.e: The GPS satellites orbit the Earth at a height of about 20,000 km. From there, they constantly send signals that a satnav receives.
115596.m: Navigation satellites orbit high above the Earth.

115598.q: How does a navigation receiver work out its distance from a satellite?
a: From the travel time of the radio signal
From the colour of the signal
With a laser beam to the satellite
From the loudness of a sound
115598.e: Each satellite sends the exact time. The distance comes from the time the signal takes to reach the receiver and the speed of light.
115598.m: Travel time times speed gives the distance.

115599.q: Why do navigation satellites carry atomic clocks?
a: Time must be measured extremely precisely
So that astronauts know the time
So that the satellites do not crash
115599.e: Even tiny time errors lead to big position errors. Atomic clocks are among the most accurate clocks there are.
115599.m: Satellite navigation needs very accurate clocks.

115600.q: A radio signal travels at 300,000 km/s. How far does it get in a millionth of a second?
115600.e: 300,000 km/s is 300,000,000 m/s. Times 0.000001 s gives 300 metres. That is why even a microsecond of clock error leads to a big mistake.
115600.m: Radio signals travel 300 metres in a microsecond.

115601.q: Apart from the satellite signal, what does a car satnav need to calculate a route?
115601.e: The satellite signal only provides the position. Only with a digital map can the device recognise roads and calculate the shortest or fastest route.
115601.m: A satnav combines position and a digital map.

115602.q: Besides temperature, what else does air conditioning often control?
115602.e: An air conditioner cools the air and removes moisture from it in the process. The first modern air conditioner, from 1902, was meant to do exactly that in a printing works.
115602.m: Air conditioning controls temperature and humidity.

115603.q: Where does the water that drips from an air conditioner come from?
a: From the moisture in the air
115603.e: The air cools down at the cold heat exchanger in the indoor unit. The water vapour in it condenses into drops, as on a cold glass.
115603.m: Air conditioners remove moisture from the air.

115604.q: Why does an air conditioner need a unit outside the room?
a: There it releases the heat outside
There it sucks in cold air
115604.e: The heat from the room has to go somewhere. The refrigerant carries it to the outdoor unit, where a fan releases it into the outside air.
115604.m: An air conditioner carries heat outside.

115605.q: How can a reversible air conditioner heat in winter?
a: It works as a heat pump
115605.e: If the cycle is reversed, the unit takes heat from the outside air and releases it in the room. It then works as a heat pump.
115605.m: A reversed air conditioner is a heat pump.

115606.q: Why does the air conditioning in a car help against misted-up windows?
115606.e: When the air cools, moisture condenses in the system. The drier air then takes up the mist from the windows.
115606.m: Dry air makes misted-up windows clear.

115607.q: How can you keep a flat cool in summer without air conditioning?
a: Close the blinds during the day and air the rooms at night
Open all the windows wide during the day
115607.e: Closed blinds keep the sun's rays out. At night the air is cooler and can cool the rooms.
115607.m: Blinds and airing at night keep rooms cool.

115608.q: Why does an air conditioner need electrical energy?
a: Heat does not flow from cool to warm by itself
Cold has to be stored in batteries
The room has to be lit
The refrigerant has to be melted
115608.e: By itself, heat always flows from a warm body to a cold one. To pump it from the cool room into the hot outside air, the compressor needs energy.
115608.m: Pumping heat the wrong way takes energy.

115609.q: In a split air conditioner, what connects the indoor unit to the outdoor unit?
a: An air shaft with fresh air
A water pipe with drinking water
A gas pipe with natural gas
115609.e: The indoor and outdoor units are connected by thin pipes in which the refrigerant circulates. So only a small hole needs to be drilled through the wall.
115609.m: In a split unit, refrigerant flows between inside and outside.

115909.q: What is meant by the nocebo effect?
a: A medicine works faster than expected
An illness heals for no reason
A doctor prescribes the wrong medicine
115909.e: If you expect something to harm you, you can really get symptoms such as a headache or nausea. The trigger is the expectation, not an active substance.
115909.m: In the nocebo effect, negative expectations cause symptoms.

115910.q: What does the Latin word “nocebo” mean?
115910.e: “Nocebo” comes from the Latin verb nocere, to harm. The form nocebo is the future tense and means “I will harm”.

115911.q: What is the counterpart of the nocebo effect called, in which positive expectations help?
115911.e: In the placebo effect, people feel better because they expect an effect. In the nocebo effect it is the other way round.
115911.m: The placebo and nocebo effects are two sides of expectation.

115912.q: How can doctors reduce nocebo effects?
a: Inform calmly and in a balanced way about risks
Describe side effects as dramatically as possible
Not talk to patients at all
115912.e: Explaining calmly how rare side effects are and what works well reduces fear. Important risks are still mentioned honestly.
115912.m: Calm and honest information can reduce nocebo effects.

115913.q: Why are people in the dummy pill group also asked about side effects in drug trials?
a: To separate real side effects from the effects of expectation
115913.e: People taking a sugar pill also often report side effects. Only by comparing can you see which symptoms really come from the active substance.
115913.m: Only comparing with the dummy pill group shows real side effects.

115914.q: What can make a nocebo effect stronger?
115914.e: If you read a long list of possible side effects and are afraid of them, you are more likely to feel such symptoms. Fear strengthens the negative expectation.
115914.m: Fear and worry can strengthen the nocebo effect.

115915.q: People next to a mobile phone mast complain of headaches, even when it has been switched off without them knowing. What best explains this?
115915.e: In such blind tests, the symptoms appeared regardless of whether the mast was really transmitting. What mattered was whether the people expected to be affected.
115915.m: Symptoms without a real cause can come from expectation.

115916.q: Is it true that symptoms from the nocebo effect are only put on?
a: Yes, they are always made up
Yes, they only happen in dreams
115916.e: Expectation affects the brain and body, for example through stress hormones. The symptoms are therefore real, even if no harmful substance is involved.
115916.m: Nocebo symptoms are real, not imagined.

115917.q: What does the ten per cent myth claim?
a: We only use 10 per cent of our brain
We sleep 10 per cent of our life
We forget 10 per cent of every day
115917.e: The myth says that 90 per cent of the brain lies unused. This idea is widespread, but wrong.
115917.m: The ten per cent myth claims we hardly use our brain.

115918.q: What does brain research say about the ten per cent myth?
a: Practically all areas of the brain are used
Only geniuses use more than 10 per cent
115918.e: Studies show that all brain regions have tasks. Over the course of the day, practically all areas are active, though not all at the same time.

115919.q: Which method can show which brain areas are active at the moment?
115919.e: Functional MRI measures where more oxygen-rich blood flows in the brain. This shows active regions, and no large unused part appears.
115919.m: Functional MRI shows which parts of the brain are working.

115920.q: Roughly how much of the body's energy does the brain use, even though it makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight?
115920.e: The brain is a very energy-hungry organ and uses about a fifth of the energy. An organ that was 90 per cent unused would be far too costly for this.
115920.m: The brain uses about a fifth of our energy.

115921.q: Which observation from medicine speaks against the ten per cent myth?
a: Even small brain injuries can have serious effects
People can live without a brain
115921.e: After a stroke in a small area, speech or movement, for example, can be affected. If 90 per cent of the area were unused, many injuries would have no effect.
115921.m: Because every brain area has a task, even small injuries cause harm.

115922.q: Why is the ten per cent myth so persistent?
a: It was proven in the laboratory
It is in every biology book
115922.e: The idea that you could awaken a huge unused potential is tempting. That is why it is often used in adverts, films and self-help books.
115922.m: The myth is popular because it promises secret superpowers.

115923.q: What would happen if all nerve cells fired at maximum at the same time?
a: You would no longer need sleep
115923.e: Healthy brain activity is finely tuned; not all cells are active at once. In an epileptic seizure, a great many nerve cells fire together out of control.
115923.m: A healthy brain works in a coordinated way, not with all cells at once.

115924.q: What is known about the origin of the ten per cent claim?
a: It is unclear; there is no study behind it
It comes from an experiment in 1990
It was announced by the WHO
It comes from a measurement on monkeys
115924.e: It is not clear who first spread the myth. In any case, there is no scientific study that supports it.
115924.m: There is no scientific evidence for the ten per cent myth.

115925.q: What are deliberately spread false reports often called?
115925.e: “Fake” means forged or false. Fake news is made-up or distorted news that looks like real reports.

115926.q: In German, which animal stands for a false report in a newspaper?
115926.e: In German, a made-up newspaper report is called a “Zeitungsente” (newspaper duck) or simply an “Ente”. Where the expression comes from is not completely clear.
115926.m: In German, a false newspaper report is called a duck.

a: A false report passed on as a warning
115927.e: A hoax is, for example, a supposed warning about a virus that you are told to send to all your contacts. This makes the false report spread further and further.
115927.m: A hoax is a false report that asks to be passed on.

115928.q: What did a large MIT study from 2018 find out about reports on Twitter?
a: False things spread faster than true things
115928.e: The researchers studied data from over ten years. False reports reached more people, and faster, probably because they seem more surprising.
115928.m: False reports often spread faster online than the truth.

115929.q: What makes satire different from a false report?
a: Satire wants to exaggerate in an obvious way
Satire only appears on the radio
115929.e: Satire exaggerates on purpose to make people laugh or think, and does not want to deceive. But if it is misunderstood, it can still be passed on as a false report.
115929.m: Satire exaggerates on purpose and does not want to deceive.

115930.q: What is a sensational headline mainly meant to get you to click on called?
115930.e: “Clickbait” is bait to make you click. Such headlines often promise more than the article delivers.
115930.m: Clickbait lures you to click with exaggerated headlines.

115931.q: What are automatically controlled accounts that spread posts on social networks in huge numbers called?
115931.e: Social bots are programs that seem like real users. They can share false reports very often in a short time.
115931.m: Social bots are programs that post like people.

115932.q: Which famous BBC April Fool's joke from 1957 was set in Ticino?
115932.e: The programme “Panorama” showed women supposedly picking spaghetti from trees. Many viewers believed it and asked how to plant spaghetti trees.
115932.m: Even serious broadcasters can fool many people with an April Fool's joke.

a: Mainly noticing what supports your own opinion
115933.e: People often look for, remember and interpret information so that it fits their own opinion. Contradicting evidence tends to be overlooked.
115933.m: With confirmation bias, we prefer what fits our own opinion.

115935.q: A football fan mainly remembers refereeing mistakes against his team. Which thinking error does this show?
115935.e: The fan believes the referee is against his team and remembers matching scenes especially well. Decisions in favour of his team stand out less to him.
115935.m: We remember especially well what fits our opinion.

115936.q: What is it called when algorithms show a person almost only content that fits their views?
115936.e: Platforms often show what you have liked before. So you see other opinions less and less, which strengthens confirmation bias.
115936.m: In a filter bubble, you see almost only what confirms your views.

115937.q: What is a group called in which everyone reinforces each other's opinions and opposing voices are missing?
115937.e: In an echo chamber, your own opinion bounces back like an echo. This makes it seem more certain than it perhaps is.
115937.m: In an echo chamber, you only hear the echo of your own opinion.

115938.q: In Peter Wason's number puzzle “2, 4, 6”, most people only tested sequences that confirmed their guess. Which thinking error did this show?
115938.e: The rule was simply “numbers going up”. Anyone who only checked confirming examples such as 8, 10, 12 hardly found the real rule, because they never tried to disprove it.
115938.m: If you only look for confirmation, you often do not find the truth.

115939.q: What helps most against confirmation bias?
115939.e: If you deliberately look for evidence against your own opinion, you test it more honestly. That is also how science works.
115939.m: Looking for counter-evidence helps against confirmation bias.

115940.q: Many people believe that A&E departments are busier at full moon. Why does this belief persist, even though studies find no link?
a: Hectic full-moon nights are remembered better
There are more doctors at full moon
It is always hot at full moon
115940.e: A hectic full-moon night fits the expectation and is remembered well. Quiet full-moon nights and hectic nights without a full moon are easily forgotten.

115941.q: What is typical of a conspiracy theory?
a: A secret plan by a group is supposed to explain everything
It is based on many measurements
115941.e: Conspiracy theories explain events by saying that a powerful group secretly controls everything. Evidence for this is usually missing.
115941.m: Conspiracy theories see a secret plan behind events.

115942.q: How do believers in conspiracy theories often react to counter-evidence?
a: They see it as part of the conspiracy
They change their minds at once
They ask for more evidence and check it
115942.e: Counter-evidence is then seen as a forgery by the conspirators. This means the theory can no longer be disproved at all.
115942.m: Conspiracy theories make themselves immune to being disproved.

115943.q: Which basic assumption is typical of conspiracy stories?
115943.e: In conspiracy stories, everything is planned and connected. Chance or simple mistakes are rejected as an explanation.
115943.m: Conspiracy stories do not accept chance.

115944.q: Which piece of evidence shows that people really were on the moon?
a: Laser reflectors left there are still targeted today
The moon can be seen from Earth
There is moon rock in every garden
115944.e: The Apollo astronauts set up mirrors on the moon. Observatories still send laser beams there today and so measure the distance to the moon.
115944.m: Mirrors from the Apollo missions on the moon prove the landings.

115945.q: What are the white trails behind aeroplanes mainly made of?
115945.e: The exhaust gases of the engines contain water vapour, which freezes into ice crystals in the cold air. Whether a trail stays for a long time depends on the humidity.

115946.q: Why do some people believe in conspiracy theories especially in uncertain times?
115946.e: In crises, many people feel helpless. A simple story with clear culprits seems to give support and a feeling of control.
115946.m: Simple explanations are especially tempting in crises.

115947.q: Why are huge secret conspiracies with thousands of people involved unlikely?
a: With many people in the know, someone is sure to give something away
115947.e: The more people are in on it, the greater the risk that someone talks or evidence turns up. That is why big secrets can hardly be kept for long.
115947.m: The more people know, the harder it is to keep something secret.

115948.q: How does the Watergate affair in the USA differ from a conspiracy theory?
a: It took place in the Middle Ages
115948.e: In the early 1970s, journalists revealed that staff of President Nixon had carried out illegal actions. Courts and investigations confirmed this.
115948.m: Real conspiracies are uncovered with evidence that can be checked.

115949.q: What is a person or group called who is blamed for a misfortune without proof?
115949.e: Conspiracy stories often look for someone to blame for crises. Blaming people like this can lead to hatred of innocent people.
115949.m: A scapegoat is blamed for misfortune without proof.

a: A teaching that seems scientific but is not
A particularly new field of research
115950.e: “Pseudo” means false or pretended. Pseudosciences use technical words but do not follow methods that can be checked.
115950.m: Pseudoscience looks scientific but does not work that way.

115951.q: What does “cherry picking” mean with evidence?
a: Picking out only the data that fits
Collecting data as completely as possible
115951.e: As when picking cherries, you take only the best pieces. Data that does not fit is left out so that the result seems more convincing.
115951.m: Showing only data that fits is cherry picking.

115952.e: Science makes its methods public and can be checked. Pseudoscience often avoids tests or explains away failures afterwards.
115952.m: Avoiding checks is not working scientifically.

115954.q: Which 19th-century teaching wanted to read a person's character from the shape of their skull?
115954.e: Phrenology claimed that bumps on the skull revealed character traits. It was disproved and is seen as an example of pseudoscience.
115954.m: Phrenology could not read anything about character from skull shapes.

115955.q: Which historical teaching tried to turn base metals into gold?
115955.e: For centuries, alchemists searched for the “philosopher's stone”. They could not make gold, but their laboratory work helped chemistry to develop.

115956.q: Is there anything in the widespread belief that Mozart's music makes babies permanently more intelligent?
a: There is no evidence for it
It only works permanently in adults
It only works with classical music by Bach
115956.e: A study from 1993 found only a brief improvement in a spatial task among students. A lasting increase in babies' intelligence has never been shown.
115956.m: Listening to Mozart is fun but does not make you permanently cleverer.

a: Individual personal stories used as proof
115957.e: A sentence like “It helped my aunt” is an anecdote. Individual cases can be chance and therefore do not prove a general effect.
115957.m: Individual stories are not scientific proof.

115958.q: What is the difference between astronomy and astrology?
a: Astronomy studies heavenly bodies, astrology interprets fates
Astrology is the older name for space travel
115958.e: Astronomy is a natural science that measures and studies stars and planets. Astrology claims the stars influence people, for which there is no evidence.
115958.m: Astronomy is science, astrology is interpretation.

115959.q: How many signs of the zodiac does Western astrology have?
115959.e: Astrology divides the zodiac into twelve equal sections of 30 degrees each, from Aries to Pisces.
115959.m: Western astrology has twelve signs of the zodiac.

115960.q: Which constellation does the Sun also pass through, even though it is not a sign of the zodiac in astrology?
115960.e: Every year the Sun also passes through Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, from about the end of November to mid-December. Astrology does not take it into account.
115960.m: The Sun travels through 13 constellations, not just 12.

115961.q: Why is the Sun on your birthday today usually no longer in the constellation of your own star sign?
a: The Earth's axis has slowly shifted over 2000 years
The Sun is getting faster and faster
115961.e: The Earth's axis wobbles very slowly like a spinning top. Since the star signs were fixed about 2000 years ago, the sky has therefore shifted by almost a whole constellation.
115961.m: Star signs and constellations no longer match today.

115962.q: Why do many people find their horoscope surprisingly accurate?
a: The statements are so general that they fit almost everyone
Horoscopes are measured for each person individually
115962.e: Sentences like “You are sometimes unsure of yourself” fit almost everyone. In an experiment, most students found the same text very accurate as their very own personal profile.
115962.m: General statements often seem surprisingly personal.

115963.q: What do scientific tests show in which astrologers have to match horoscopes to the right people?
a: Their hits are no better than chance
They are only right with children
They are only right at full moon
115963.e: In such blind tests, the astrologers do not know whose horoscope is whose. They are not right more often than by pure guessing.
115963.m: In controlled tests, astrology predicts no more than chance.

115964.q: What does a horoscope originally show?
a: The positions of the heavenly bodies at a point in time
The weather forecast for a week
The Sun's path around the Earth
115964.e: A horoscope is a drawing that records the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, for example at birth. Astrology interprets character and fate from it.
115964.m: A horoscope shows the sky at a particular moment.

115965.q: Which famous astronomer also made horoscopes to earn money?
115965.e: Kepler discovered the laws of planetary orbits. Because horoscopes were in demand at the time, he also wrote them and partly paid his living costs that way.
115965.m: Even great astronomers used to write horoscopes for money.

115966.q: What do people want to find with a dowsing rod?
115966.e: Traditionally, people use a dowsing rod to search for underground water, ores or supposed “earth rays”.
115966.m: A dowsing rod is mainly used to search for water.

115967.q: What shape is a classic dowsing rod?
115967.e: The rod is held at both ends with tense hands. Modern rods are often bent wires or metal rods too.
115967.m: The classic dowsing rod is a forked branch.

115968.q: What are people called who search with a dowsing rod?
115968.e: Dowsers walk slowly across an area and watch for the rod to move. There is no scientifically recognised training for this.
115968.m: Someone who searches with a dowsing rod is called a dowser.

115969.q: What best explains why a dowsing rod moves?
115969.e: In the ideomotor effect, the muscles move very slightly without you noticing. The tense rod amplifies these small movements into a clear swing.
115969.m: The rod moves because of unconscious hand movements.

115970.q: Why do dowsers often seem successful when looking for water?
a: In many areas you find groundwater almost everywhere
115970.e: In central Europe, in many areas there is groundwater almost everywhere at a certain depth. A hit therefore does not prove that the rod works.
115970.m: Hits are no proof if you find water almost everywhere.

115971.q: How does groundwater usually occur in the ground?
a: In huge cave lakes under every town
115971.e: Groundwater usually fills the pores and cracks of gravel, sand or rock over large areas. Narrow “water veins”, as dowsers describe them, are the exception.
115971.m: Groundwater usually lies in wide layers, not narrow veins.

115972.q: How can you fairly test whether a person finds water with a dowsing rod?
a: With a blind test using hidden water pipes
115972.e: In a blind test, neither the person nor the observer knows which hidden pipe water is flowing through. Only this shows whether the hit rate is above chance.
115972.m: Only blind tests show whether an ability really exists.

115973.q: What happened to the one million dollar prize that the James Randi Educational Foundation offered for proof of supernatural abilities?
115973.e: Many applicants, including dowsers, came to be tested. None could show their ability under controlled conditions.
115973.m: Under controlled conditions, nobody could prove supernatural powers.

115974.q: Looked at closely, what shape is the Earth?
a: A sphere slightly flattened at the poles
115974.e: Because it spins, the Earth is a little wider at the equator than from pole to pole. The difference between the diameters is about 43 km.
115974.m: The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles.

115975.q: Which observation did Aristotle give as a sign that the Earth is round?
a: The round shadow of the Earth during lunar eclipses
115975.e: In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the moon and is always round. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every direction.
115975.m: The Earth's round shadow on the moon reveals its shape.

115976.q: What do you see when a ship at sea sails far away?
a: It disappears from the bottom up
It just gets smaller and smaller
It disappears from the top down
115976.e: Because of the Earth's curve, the hull disappears behind the horizon first and the top of the mast last. On a flat Earth, the ship would simply get smaller.
115976.m: Because of the Earth's curve, ships disappear from the bottom first.

115977.q: Is it true that scholars in the Middle Ages thought the Earth was a disc?
a: No, they knew it was round
Yes, they all thought it was flat
No, they thought it was a cube
115977.e: Since ancient times, educated people knew the Earth was a sphere. The idea that the Middle Ages believed in a disc is itself a myth from later times.
115977.m: Medieval scholars knew that the Earth is a sphere.

115978.q: What was the argument before Columbus's voyage in 1492 really about?
115978.e: Columbus thought the Earth was far too small and the route to Asia too short. His critics were right that Asia was too far away.
115978.m: Columbus was wrong about the size of the Earth, not its shape.

115979.q: Which expedition was the first to sail around the whole world, from 1519 to 1522?
115979.e: Ferdinand Magellan died on the way, but Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage with one ship. The journey around the world confirmed in practice that the Earth is round.
115979.m: Magellan's expedition was the first to sail around the Earth.

115980.q: Why is it still early morning in New York when it is already midday in Zurich?
a: Because the Sun only lights up half of the spinning globe
Because New York is higher up
Because the clocks in the USA are wrong
Because the Sun is closer in Europe
115980.e: The Earth spins, and only one half of the globe faces the Sun at any time. That is why there are time zones, which could not be explained on a flat disc.
115980.m: Time zones exist because the Earth spins.

115981.q: Roughly how long is the Earth's circumference at the equator?
115981.e: The circumference at the equator is about 40,075 km. The metre was originally defined so that a quarter of a meridian is 10,000 km long.
115981.m: The Earth measures about 40,000 km around the equator.

115982.q: What do astronauts see from the ISS space station at a height of about 400 km?
a: The curved surface of the Earth
A wall of ice around the world
115982.e: From the ISS the horizon is clearly curved. The station circles the Earth about every 90 minutes.
115982.m: From space you can clearly see that the Earth is round.

115983.q: What do you do in a fact check?
a: You check whether a claim is true
115983.e: In a fact check, statements are compared with reliable sources and data. The result can be true, false or misleading.
115983.m: A fact check tests claims against evidence.

115984.q: How can you find out where and when a photo first appeared on the internet?
115984.e: In a reverse search, you upload the image to a search engine. This shows whether an old image is being spread again in the wrong context.
115984.m: A reverse image search shows where a photo comes from.

115985.q: A supposed quote from a famous person goes viral. What is a sensible step to check it?
a: Look for the original source of the quote
Look at the number of likes
115985.e: Many quotes are falsely put into the mouths of famous people. Only a book, speech or interview as a source shows whether someone really said it.
115985.m: A quote is only believable once you know its source.

115986.q: What is the best way to check an unfamiliar website?
a: Read what other sources say about it
See whether it is nicely designed
Believe it if it is at the top of the search results
115986.e: Instead of just staying on the site, you look in other tabs to see who is behind it. Professional fact-checkers work this way too.
115986.m: It is best to check a source from the outside.

115987.q: Which hidden information in a photo file can reveal when and with what a picture was taken?
115987.e: Cameras and phones often store the date, the device and sometimes the location in the file. But this metadata can also be missing or changed.
115987.m: Metadata reveals a lot about where a photo comes from.

115988.q: A risk rises from 1 to 2 cases per 10,000 people. By how much has the risk risen in absolute terms?
115988.e: 1 in 10,000 is 0.01 per cent, 2 in 10,000 is 0.02 per cent. So the rise is only 0.01 percentage points, even though the risk has “doubled”.
115988.m: Doubling can mean very little with small numbers.

115989.q: In summer, ice cream sales and swimming accidents rise at the same time. What follows from this?
a: Both have a common cause, the heat
Swimming accidents make you want ice cream
115989.e: Two things that rise together are not necessarily cause and effect. Here, the warm weather leads to more ice cream and more swimmers.
115989.m: Rising together does not prove a cause.

115990.q: Why should you read more than just the headline before sharing an article?
115990.e: A headline has to be short and eye-catching, so it often leaves out important things. Only the whole text shows what is really being claimed.
115990.m: Read the whole article before sharing it.

a: Checking the origin and credibility of a source
Rating a source as badly as possible
115991.e: In source criticism, you ask who wrote something, when, where and with what intention. Only then can you judge how reliable a piece of information is.
115991.m: Source criticism means checking where information comes from.

115992.q: A diary from 1940 is read in a history lesson. What kind of source is it?
115992.e: Primary sources come directly from the time being studied. A school book that reports on that time would be a secondary source.
115992.m: Primary sources come from the time in question.

115993.q: Where on a website do you find who is responsible for the content?
115993.e: Serious websites give the names and contact details of those responsible in the legal notice. If there is none, be careful.
115993.m: The legal notice shows who is behind a website.

115994.q: What is the best way to check a statement in a Wikipedia article?
115994.e: Wikipedia articles are supposed to back up their statements with evidence. The references lead you to the original source.
115994.m: On Wikipedia, it is worth looking at the references.

115995.q: What does the label “Ad” or “Sponsored” on a post mean?
115995.e: Such posts were paid for by a company. They are mainly meant to sell and are therefore not neutral.
115995.m: Sponsored posts are adverts and not neutral.

115996.q: A study on sugary drinks was paid for by a drinks maker. What should you pay special attention to?
115996.e: Whoever pays for a study often has an interest in a particular result. The study is not automatically wrong, but it should be checked especially carefully.
115996.m: With paid-for studies, check for conflicts of interest.

115997.q: Why is the publication date of a source important?
a: Older information can be out of date
115997.e: Figures, records or research results change over time. An old article may therefore no longer be true today.
115997.m: With every source, check how up to date it is.

115998.q: Which question is NOT one of the typical questions of source criticism?
a: How many likes does the post have?
With what intention was it made?
115998.e: The number of likes only shows how popular a post is, not whether it is true. What matters is the author, the time and the intention.

a: Checking of a study by independent experts
A rating in the app store
115999.e: Before a journal publishes a study, other experts read it critically. They look for mistakes and often ask for improvements.
115999.m: In peer review, experts check the work of other experts.

116000.q: What does the word “peer” mean in peer review?
116000.e: The reviewers are researchers from the same field. So they are “equals” of the authors.
116000.m: Peers are experts at the same level.

116001.q: What does double-blind peer review mean?
a: Reviewers and researchers do not know each other's names
The study is checked in the dark
116001.e: This is so that fame, friendship or rivalry does not influence the judgement. Only the work itself is assessed.
116001.m: In double-blind peer review, both sides stay anonymous.

116002.e: Preprints make results available quickly, for example during a crisis. But they have not yet been checked by experts, so they should be read with caution.
116002.m: Preprints are studies that have not yet been reviewed.

116003.q: What can peer review NOT guarantee?
a: That a result is definitely correct
116003.e: Reviewers only see the submitted manuscript and cannot repeat every experiment. Mistakes or even fraud can therefore go undetected.
116003.m: Peer review reduces mistakes, but does not make results infallible.

116004.q: What is it called when other researchers repeat an experiment to check the result?
116004.e: A result is considered especially reliable if independent teams confirm it several times. If it cannot be repeated, caution is needed.
116004.m: Repeated experiments make knowledge more certain.

116005.q: What happens to a published study if serious mistakes or deception are found later?
116005.e: In 2010, for example, the journal “The Lancet” withdrew a 1998 study that had claimed a false link between vaccination and autism.

116006.q: Which journal is a well-known example of a peer-reviewed journal?
116006.e: “Nature” has been published since 1869 and publishes research from all the natural sciences. Submitted papers are reviewed by experts.
116006.m: Major journals have studies checked before they are printed.

116007.q: What are publishers called that publish almost anything for payment without real review?
116007.e: Predatory publishers pretend to be serious academic journals but hardly check the papers. Their articles are therefore less trustworthy.
116007.m: Not every journal with a scientific name really checks.

117304.q: Why is the door handle placed as far as possible from the hinges?
a: A long lever arm needs less force
It makes the door close faster
117304.e: For the same turning effect, a smaller force is enough if you are further from the pivot. That is why a door is easy to open at its outer edge.
117304.m: A long lever arm saves force.

120555.q: How does the siren of an ambulance coming towards you sound?
a: Higher than when it is still
Lower than when it is still
120555.e: As it approaches, the wave crests arrive at shorter intervals. So the listener hears a higher frequency.
120555.m: An approaching sound source sounds higher.

120560.q: Which animals use the frequency shift of their ultrasound echoes to locate prey?
120560.e: Some bats, such as horseshoe bats, analyse the Doppler shift of their calls. This lets them detect things like fluttering insect wings.
120560.m: Bats also locate prey with the help of the Doppler effect.

121627.q: Which native bird is a well-known brood parasite?
121627.e: The female cuckoo lays her eggs in other birds' nests. The host birds raise the cuckoo chick, often at the expense of their own young.
121627.m: The cuckoo has its young raised by other birds.

123401.q: Which plants are typical of the Arctic tundra?
123401.e: Only low plants that can cope with cold and a short growing season grow in the tundra. Dwarf willows and dwarf birches hardly reach knee height.
123401.m: The tundra is dominated by mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs.

124408.q: What colour is grade A on the Nutri-Score?
124408.e: A is dark green and stands for the best nutritional composition. E is red.
124408.m: A dark green A is the best Nutri-Score grade.

125400.q: Where does the energy stored in biomass originally come from?
a: From geothermal heat deep inside the Earth
From nuclear fission in the ground
125400.e: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy and store it in sugar, starch and cellulose. This energy is released again when it is burnt.

126114.q: The fruits of which plant served as George de Mestral's model?
126114.e: Burdock fruits have lots of tiny hooks and get caught in fur and clothes. This is how animals spread their seeds.
126114.m: Burdock was the model for Velcro.

126120.q: Which two parts does a Velcro fastener consist of?
126120.e: One strip has tiny hooks, the other soft loops. When pressed together they hook into each other; when pulled apart they come undone again.
126120.m: A Velcro fastener consists of hooks and loops.

126163.e: Urban gardening means growing vegetables, herbs and flowers in cities. It is often done together with others on waste ground, roofs or in backyards.
126163.m: Urban gardening is gardening in the city.

126179.q: Which winter road treatment is especially harmful to city trees along roads?
126179.e: Road salt gets into the soil with meltwater and damages roots and leaves. The trees then take up water and nutrients less well.
126179.m: Road salt harms the roots of city trees.

126393.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance emergency line when an ambulance needs to go to hospital?
126393.e: 144 is the number for the ambulance emergency line. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 143 the helpline Dargebotene Hand.
126393.m: In Switzerland you dial 144 for an ambulance.

127571.q: What do people do in bionics?
a: Count the stars in the sky
127571.e: In bionics, researchers look closely at how animals and plants solve problems. Then they use these ideas for new technology.

127573.q: Which plant was the model for Velcro?
127573.e: Burdock burrs easily get caught on clothes and fur. Velcro holds in exactly the same way.
127573.m: Velcro was copied from the burdock.

127574.q: Which country did the inventor of Velcro come from?
127574.e: The engineer George de Mestral came from the canton of Vaud. He had his invention protected in the middle of the 20th century.
127574.m: Velcro was invented by a Swiss man.

127575.q: Where did the inventor of Velcro discover lots of burrs?
127575.e: After a walk, lots of burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. He looked at them closely under the microscope.
127575.m: A walk with the dog gave him the idea for Velcro.

127576.q: What does a burr have on its spines?
127576.e: The spines of the burr end in little hooks. With them, they catch in fur or fabric.
127576.m: A burr holds on with tiny hooks.

127577.q: What does the second side of a Velcro fastener have, which the hooks catch in?
127577.e: One side of the Velcro has hooks, the other lots of soft loops. If you press them together, they catch on each other.
127577.m: Hooks and loops hold Velcro together.

127578.q: What does a bionics expert do first?
127578.e: First you have to understand how an animal or plant does something. Only then can you turn the idea into technology.
127578.m: People who work in bionics observe nature first.

127579.q: What does water do on a lotus leaf?
127579.e: The lotus leaf is water-repellent. Drops of water simply roll over it.
127579.m: Water rolls off a lotus leaf in beads.

127580.q: What do the rolling water drops take with them from the lotus leaf?
127580.e: The rolling drops collect dust and dirt and carry them away. This makes the leaf clean.
127580.m: Water drops wash the lotus leaf clean.

127581.q: What is it called when a leaf keeps itself clean?
127581.e: With the lotus, rain is enough to make the leaf clean again. This is called self-cleaning.
127581.m: The lotus leaf can clean itself.

127582.q: What does the surface of a lotus leaf have when you magnify it a lot?
127582.e: Under the microscope you can see lots of tiny bumps. Drops only touch them in a few places.
127582.m: Tiny bumps make the lotus leaf water-repellent.

127583.q: What else is the lotus leaf covered with?
127583.e: A fine layer of wax repels water. Together with the bumps, this creates the lotus effect.
127583.m: Fine wax helps the lotus leaf repel water.

127584.q: Where does the lotus plant grow?
127584.e: The lotus is a water plant and grows in ponds and lakes. Its large leaves lie on the water or stick up above it.
127584.m: The lotus is a water plant.

127585.q: Which product uses the lotus effect?
127585.e: There are outdoor wall paints with a surface like a lotus leaf. Rain washes the dirt off the wall of the house.
127585.m: Some house paints stay clean thanks to the lotus effect.

127586.q: What colour is the flower of the lotus plant often?
127586.e: The large flowers of the lotus are often pink, sometimes white too. They stick up high above the water.
127586.m: The lotus often has large pink flowers.

127587.q: What shape is a water drop on a lotus leaf?
127587.e: Because the leaf repels the water, the drop pulls together almost into a ball. That way it can roll off easily.
127587.m: On a lotus leaf, drops become almost perfectly round.

127588.q: What does shark skin feel like when you stroke it from the tail to the head?
127588.e: A shark's skin is covered in tiny hard scales. That is why it feels rough when you stroke it the wrong way.
127588.m: Stroked the wrong way, shark skin is rough.

127589.q: What is the surface of shark skin made of?
127589.e: A shark's scales look like little teeth. That is why they are called skin teeth.
127589.m: A shark has tiny teeth on its skin.

127590.q: What do the fine grooves on shark skin help with?
a: Gliding through the water more easily
127590.e: The grooves on the skin teeth guide the water and reduce drag. So the shark swims using less strength.
127590.m: Shark skin helps the shark glide easily through the water.

127591.q: Which sportswear was made with shark skin as a model?
127591.e: Swimsuits with a surface like shark skin were meant to reduce drag in the water. The idea was to swim faster.
127591.m: There were swimsuits modelled on shark skin.

127592.q: What is a ship's paint modelled on shark skin meant to prevent?
a: Mussels and algae growing on it
127592.e: Hardly any algae or mussels settle on the skin of sharks. People want to achieve that for ships too.
127592.m: Shark skin stays free of mussels and algae.

127593.q: Which vehicles are given a film like shark skin to save fuel?
127593.e: A film with tiny grooves reduces air resistance. So aeroplanes need slightly less fuel.
127593.m: Shark-skin film helps aeroplanes save fuel.

127594.q: Which animal group do sharks belong to?
127594.e: Sharks breathe with gills and spend their whole life in water. They are fish.

127595.q: Where can a gecko even walk?
127595.e: Geckos cling so well that they can walk upside down on the ceiling. Even smooth panes of glass are no problem for them.
127595.m: A gecko can walk upside down on the ceiling.

127596.q: What does a gecko have on the underside of its toes?
127596.e: On the toes there are millions of tiny hairs. They get so close to the wall that they stick to it.
127596.m: Fine hairs let the gecko stick to walls.

127597.q: What does a gecko NOT need to stick to a pane of glass?
127597.e: The gecko sticks without any glue. It is only the tiny hairs on its toes that hold it on.
127597.m: A gecko sticks without any glue.

127598.q: Which animal group does the gecko belong to?
127598.e: Geckos are lizards and so they are reptiles. They have scaly skin.

127599.q: What have researchers developed with the gecko as a model?
a: Sticky tape that can be removed again
Glasses that see in the dark
127599.e: Modelled on gecko toes, there are sticky strips without glue. You can remove them and use them again.
127599.m: Gecko tape sticks and can be removed again.

127600.q: When are many geckos out and about?
127600.e: Many types of gecko hunt insects at night. During the day they hide.
127600.m: Many geckos are active at night.

127601.q: How does a gecko get its foot off the wall again?
127601.e: The gecko peels its toes off from the tip like sticky tape. That way it frees its foot very easily.
127601.m: A gecko peels off its toes to let go.

127602.q: What can a gecko shed when in danger?
127602.e: If an enemy grabs the gecko by the tail, it sheds it and escapes. The tail then grows back.
127602.m: A gecko can shed its tail.

127603.q: What does a spider build its web from?
127603.e: The spider makes its threads itself. The material is called spider silk.
127603.m: Spider webs are made of spider silk.

127604.q: Where on the spider are the threads made?
a: On the back part of the body
127604.e: At the end of the back part of its body, the spider has spinnerets. The silk comes out there.
127604.m: The spider spins its threads at the back of its body.

127605.q: A spider's thread is very thin. Does that make it weak?
127605.e: Spider silk is amazingly strong. For its thickness, it can take more than a steel wire of the same thinness.
127605.m: Spider silk is thin but very strong.

127606.q: What can a spider's thread do especially well without breaking?
127606.e: Spider silk is very stretchy. So the web catches a flying insect without tearing.
127606.m: Spider threads are stretchy and do not break easily.

127607.q: What is spider silk made of?
127607.e: Spider silk is made of proteins. Researchers are trying to produce these proteins artificially.
127607.m: Spider silk is made of protein.

127608.q: What would people like to use artificial spider silk for, for example?
127608.e: Spider silk is strong and the body accepts it well. So it could be used in medicine, for example for stitches.
127608.m: Artificial spider silk could help in medicine.

127609.q: Why doesn't a spider get stuck in its own web?
a: It walks on threads that are not sticky
It washes the web with water
127609.e: Not all the threads in the web are sticky. The spider walks mainly on the dry threads.
127609.m: The spider knows the dry threads in its web.

127610.q: What does a spider catch with its web?
127610.e: Flies, mosquitoes and other insects get caught in the web. The spider then eats them.
127610.m: Spiders catch insects in their webs.

127611.e: Many types of termite build large mounds. A whole colony lives inside.

127612.q: What do termites build their mounds from?
127612.e: Termites mix soil with their saliva. When the mixture dries, it becomes rock hard.
127612.m: Termite mounds are built from soil and saliva.

127613.q: What provides fresh air in a termite mound?
127613.e: Air flows through the mound through many tunnels and shafts. This keeps it pleasant inside.
127613.m: Tunnels and channels air the termite mound.

127614.q: On which continent is there a well-known office building that is aired like a termite mound?
127614.e: In Zimbabwe, a large building was built that airs itself on the model of termite mounds. That is why it needs much less energy for ventilation and cooling.
127614.m: A building in Africa airs itself like a termite mound.

127615.q: What does a building designed like a termite mound save?
127615.e: The air is cooled without big machines. That is why the building needs much less electricity.

127616.e: Termites like warmth. Most kinds live in the tropics and other warm areas.
127616.m: Termites live mainly in warm countries.

127617.q: How high can termite mounds get?
127617.e: Some termite mounds are taller than an adult. They can be several metres high.
127617.m: Termite mounds can be several metres high.

127618.e: Many termites eat wood and other plant parts. That is why they can also damage wooden houses.

127619.e: The boxfish has an angular body. It looks like a little box.
127619.m: The boxfish is square like a box.

127620.q: What surrounds the body of the boxfish?
127620.e: The boxfish lives inside a shell of bony plates. Only its fins, eyes and mouth stick out.
127620.m: The boxfish wears a hard shell.

127621.q: What was built with the boxfish as a model?
127621.e: A car maker built a test car in the shape of the boxfish. It was meant to have little air resistance.
127621.m: A car was modelled on the boxfish.

127622.q: What does the boxfish mainly swim with?
a: Its whole body like a snake
A jet of water like a squid
127622.e: The hard shell can hardly bend. That is why the boxfish moves mainly with its small fins.
127622.m: The boxfish swims with its fins.

a: In the sea near coral reefs
127623.e: Boxfish live in warm seas. They are often found near coral reefs.
127623.m: The boxfish lives in the sea near corals.

127624.q: What does the young yellow boxfish look like?
127624.e: The young yellow boxfish is bright yellow and has black spots. The colour warns enemies.
127624.m: The young yellow boxfish is yellow with black spots.

127625.q: What can the boxfish release when in danger?
127625.e: The boxfish can release poison through its skin. This protects it from enemies.
127625.m: The boxfish protects itself with poison.

127626.q: What did engineers learn from the boxfish's shell?
a: How to build light but strong
How to build as heavy as possible
How to build only with glass
How to build only round parts
127626.e: The boxfish's shell is light and yet very strong. This is also useful for cars and machines.
127626.m: The boxfish shows how to build light and strong.

127627.q: Which vehicle was given a nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak?
127627.e: Engineers in Japan shaped the front of a high-speed train like a kingfisher's beak. The kingfisher was a good model for this.
127627.m: A Japanese high-speed train has a nose like a kingfisher.

127628.q: What problem did the high-speed train in Japan used to have when leaving a tunnel?
127628.e: The train pushed the air in the tunnel along in front of it. When it came out, there was a loud bang.
127628.m: The new train nose helped against the bang at the tunnel.

127629.q: How does the kingfisher dive into the water?
127629.e: The kingfisher's beak is shaped so that it slides into the water with almost no splash. That is why it was a good model.
127629.m: The kingfisher dives in with almost no splash.

127630.q: What does the kingfisher mainly eat?
127630.e: The kingfisher sits on a branch over the water. When it sees a small fish, it plunges in.

127631.q: What colour is the kingfisher's back?
127631.e: The kingfisher has a bright blue back and an orange breast. It is one of the most colourful birds in Switzerland.
127631.m: The kingfisher has a bright blue back.

127632.q: Where can you watch kingfishers in Switzerland?
127632.e: The kingfisher needs clear water with small fish. That is why it lives by water.
127632.m: You find the kingfisher by water.

127633.q: What did the high-speed train with the kingfisher nose need less of than before?
127633.e: With the new nose, the train has to push away less air. That is why it uses less electricity.
127633.m: The kingfisher nose saves the train electricity.

127634.q: Where does the kingfisher make its nest?
a: In a tunnel in an earth bank
127634.e: The kingfisher digs a tunnel into a steep earth bank by the water. The nest is at the end of the tunnel.
127634.m: The kingfisher nests in a tunnel in the riverbank.

127635.q: What does the humpback whale have on the front edge of its flippers?
127635.e: The front edge of the flipper is not smooth but has lots of bumps. It looks like a row of lumps.
127635.m: The humpback whale's flipper has bumps.

127636.q: What do the bumps on its flippers help the humpback whale to do?
127636.e: The bumps guide the water well around the flipper. So the big whale can swim in surprisingly tight turns.
127636.m: Thanks to the bumps, the humpback whale is very agile.

127637.q: Which machines were given blades with bumps modelled on the humpback whale?
127637.e: Rotor blades with bumps like the humpback whale's are meant to use the wind better. Fans have also been built this way.
127637.m: Some wind turbines have bumps like the humpback whale.

127638.q: What is special about the humpback whale's flippers?
127638.e: The humpback whale has the longest flippers of all whales. They are about a third as long as its body.
127638.m: The humpback whale has very long flippers.

127639.q: Which animal group does the humpback whale belong to?
127639.e: Whales breathe with lungs and feed their young with milk. That is why they are mammals, even though they live in the sea.
127639.m: The humpback whale is a mammal.

127640.q: What are humpback whales famous for?
127640.e: Male humpback whales sing long songs made of many sounds. They can be heard far away underwater.

127641.q: What does the humpback whale eat?
127641.e: The humpback whale has no teeth, but baleen plates. With them, it sieves krill and small fish out of the water.
127641.m: The humpback whale eats krill and small fish.

127642.q: How does the humpback whale drive fish together into a shoal?
a: With a net of air bubbles
127642.e: The humpback whale swims in a circle and blows out air bubbles. The fish stay trapped in this bubble net.
127642.m: Humpback whales hunt with a net of air bubbles.

127643.q: What does a streamlined shape look like?
a: Round at the front and narrow at the back
Flat at the front and wide at the back
127643.e: A body that is round at the front and gets narrower towards the back glides well through air and water. This shape is called streamlined.
127643.m: A streamlined shape is round at the front and narrow at the back.

127644.q: Which bird swims very fast underwater thanks to its streamlined shape?
127644.e: The penguin has a smooth, spindle-shaped body. With it, it shoots through the water like a torpedo.
127644.m: The penguin is a fast swimmer.

127645.q: Why are vehicles often built with a streamlined shape?
127645.e: A streamlined shape is slowed down less by the air. That is why a vehicle needs less fuel or electricity.

127646.q: Which shape is thought to be especially good for gliding through the air?
127646.e: A falling drop is round at the front and pointed at the back. This shape gives the air very little resistance.
127646.m: The teardrop shape glides well through the air.

127647.q: What slows you down when you ride your bike fast, even when there is no wind?
a: The air you have to push away
127647.e: When you ride, the bike has to push the air aside. The faster you go, the more this air slows you down. This is called air resistance.
127647.m: Air resistance slows you down when cycling.

127648.q: Why do racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars?
a: So less air slows them down
So they can see the road better
So the saddle is more comfortable
127648.e: If you crouch down, you give the air a smaller surface. That way the headwind slows you down less.
127648.m: Crouching makes you faster because less air slows you down.

127649.q: Which fish is a fast swimmer with a streamlined shape?
127649.e: The tuna has a spindle-shaped body like a torpedo. It is one of the fastest fish.
127649.m: Thanks to its shape, the tuna is a fast swimmer.

127650.q: Where do people test how much a car is slowed down by the wind?
127650.e: In a wind tunnel, a strong wind blows at the car. This shows how the air flows past it.
127650.m: Air resistance is tested in a wind tunnel.

127651.q: Which famous artist drew flying machines modelled on birds more than 500 years ago?
127651.e: Leonardo da Vinci watched birds closely and drew flying machines. But they could not fly yet.
127651.m: Leonardo da Vinci dreamed of flying like a bird.

127652.q: Which bird did the flight pioneer Otto Lilienthal study especially closely?
127652.e: Otto Lilienthal studied how storks fly. Then he built flying machines and flew them himself.
127652.m: Otto Lilienthal learned from the stork.

127653.q: How is a bird’s wing shaped, much like an aeroplane wing?
127653.e: The wing is curved on top. When air flows over it, an upward force called lift is created.
127653.m: A curved wing lifts birds and aeroplanes into the air.

127654.q: What do many aeroplanes have at their wingtips, copied from birds?
127654.e: Birds of prey spread the feathers at the ends of their wings and bend them upwards. Bent wingtips on aeroplanes also save fuel.
127654.m: Aeroplanes copied bent wingtips from birds.

127655.q: Which bird flies almost silently and was the model for quiet fans?
127655.e: An owl’s feathers have fine fringes along the edge. That is why you can hardly hear it fly, and fans built this way are quieter too.

127656.q: Why do migrating birds such as geese often fly in a V shape?
127656.e: Each bird uses the rising air from the bird in front of it. That way they all save energy on the long journey.
127656.m: Flying in a V shape saves migrating birds energy.

127657.q: What makes many bird bones especially light?
127657.e: Many bird bones are hollow inside and supported by thin struts. This makes them light but still strong.

127658.q: What is it called when a bird floats through the air without flapping its wings?
127658.e: When gliding, the bird keeps its wings still and slowly floats downwards. This saves energy.
127658.m: When gliding, a bird does not flap its wings.

127659.q: What does a cone do when the weather is dry?
127659.e: In dry air the scales spread apart. In damp weather they close again.
127659.m: A cone opens when it is dry.

127660.q: Why does a cone open in dry weather?
a: So the seeds can fly away
So birds can live in it
127660.e: The seeds have little wings. In dry weather the wind carries them far away.
127660.m: The cone opens so the wind can spread the seeds.

127661.q: What does a cone need to open and close?
127661.e: A cone still moves even when it fell from the tree a long time ago. It does not need muscles for this, only dry or damp air.

127662.q: Why do the scales of a cone bend?
a: Two layers swell by different amounts
127662.e: Each scale has two layers. When it is damp, one layer expands more than the other, so the scale bends.
127662.m: Two different layers make the scale bend.

127663.q: Which idea for clothing was copied from cones?
a: Fabric that opens air holes when you sweat
Fabric that glows in the dark
127663.e: Like the scales of a cone, tiny flaps in the fabric can open when it gets damp. This lets more air reach the skin.
127663.m: Clothing modelled on cones airs itself.

127664.q: Where are the seeds in a cone?
127664.e: The seeds lie protected under each scale. They can only get out once the scale opens.
127664.m: The seeds lie under the scales of the cone.

127665.q: How do the cones of the silver fir sit on the branch?
127665.e: The cones of the silver fir stand upright on the branches. They fall apart up there and do not drop down whole.
127665.m: Fir cones stand upright on the branch.

127666.q: Which tree do most of the cones you find on the ground in a Swiss forest come from?
127666.e: Spruce cones hang down and fall to the ground whole. Even so, many people call them “fir cones”.
127666.m: The cones on the forest floor are usually spruce cones.

127667.q: Which animal likes to get the seeds out of cones?
127667.e: The squirrel gnaws off the scales and eats the seeds. What is left is a gnawed core.
127667.m: Squirrels eat the seeds from cones.

127668.q: Where is the water pressure in a lake greatest?
a: Right at the top at the surface
127668.e: The deeper you dive, the more water there is above you. This water pushes down with its weight.
127668.m: The deeper the water, the greater the pressure.

127669.q: A cup has a hole near the top and a hole near the bottom on its side. From which hole does the water spray further?
127669.e: There is more water above the bottom hole, so the pressure there is greater. The water is pushed out more strongly.
127669.m: At the bottom of the cup, the water pushes harder than at the top.

127670.q: A house has a tap on the ground floor and one on the top floor. Where does the water usually come out with more pressure?
127670.e: The water on the ground floor has more water in the pipe above it. So it pushes harder there than at the very top.
127670.m: Water pressure is greater at the bottom of a house than at the top.

127671.q: Where does the pressure in the water of a swimming pool come from?
127671.e: Water is heavy. The water higher up pushes on the water further down.
127671.m: The weight of the water creates water pressure.

127672.q: From which side does water push on a diver?
127672.e: Water pushes in all directions at once. That is why a diver feels the pressure all around.

127673.q: A full water bag has a small hole. What happens if you squeeze the bag hard?
a: The water squirts out more strongly
127673.e: When you squeeze, the pressure in the bag gets bigger. The water is pushed through the hole faster.
127673.m: More pressure makes the water squirt harder.

127674.q: Why do submarines have very thick, strong walls?
a: So the water pressure doesn't crush them
127674.e: In the deep, a huge amount of water presses on the submarine. Strong walls can withstand this pressure.
127674.m: Deep in the sea, a submarine needs very strong walls.

127675.q: What can you use to measure the pressure in a water pipe?
127675.e: A pressure gauge shows how hard the water in the pipe is pushing. A thermometer, on the other hand, measures warmth.
127675.m: Water pressure is measured with a pressure gauge.

127676.q: What happens to an empty plastic bottle with the lid screwed on if you push it deep into water?
127676.e: In the deep, the water pushes hard on the outside of the bottle. The air inside is squeezed and the bottle gets dents.

127677.q: What is the famous big fountain in Geneva called?
127677.e: The Jet d'eau stands in Lake Geneva and is a landmark of Geneva. The name is French and means ‘water jet’.
127677.m: The Jet d'eau is the landmark of Geneva.

127678.q: Roughly how high does the Jet d'eau in Geneva spray?
127678.e: Powerful pumps push the water about 140 metres into the air. That is higher than most church towers.
127678.m: The Jet d'eau sprays higher than a church tower.

127679.q: What does a modern fountain need to make the water spray up?
127679.e: The pump pushes the water up through the nozzle with force. Without a pump, the water would just lie there.
